title: Admissibility-Preserving Control for Block Strict-Feedback Systems Under Time-Varying Asymmetric Actuator and State Constraints
summary: This paper addresses the tracking control of block strict-feedback nonlinear systems subject to time-varying asymmetric actuator and full state constraints. To that end, we develop a time-varying Admissibility-Preserving Control (APC) framework, in which the Admissibility-Preserving Input Realization (APIR) generates the plant input through a dynamic realization. The APIR guarantees input admissibility under the moving actuator set whenever each actuator bound contracts slower than the decay rate of the realization, and a closed-form lower bound on its gain is derived. The state constraints are handled by a logarithmic barrier coordinate at every backstepping step, with widths measured from the virtual control to the moving envelope of the corresponding state. We prove that every state lies inside its envelope, with each virtual control only required to remain inside the envelope of the next state, while the tracking error converges to zero exponentially. Simulations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed safety-critical control scheme.

title: Physical-Risk-Aware Decentralized Agents for Constrained Vehicle Communications
summary: Decentralized V2X resource control is challenging because each vehicle has only local observations, while reliability depends on network-wide interactions. We develop a physical-risk-aware spatio-temporal graph attention (PA-STGAT) framework for agentic V2X control. Each vehicle perceives its local interaction graph, retains short-term temporal context, and independently selects its PC5 resource and power. Network outcomes are used during centralized training to refine the shared policy. Transmitter-specific credits map reliability failures to individual vehicles. A dual-priced graph term further converts network violations into coordination signals for discrete resource selection, with higher priority on short time-to-collision links. Experiments show higher raw-policy reliability than the tested graph-based baselines. Under filtered execution, PA-STGAT meets the nominal empirical communication requirements across all five seeds, with tradeoffs among utility, delivery reliability, resource occupancy, and filter-induced repair. Compared with GNN+MATD3, it requires fewer resource repairs but achieves lower utility and mean delivery reliability. Mechanism ablations show that removing dual-priced graph coordination causes resource-selection collapse. Density and mobility tests characterize the operating limits of empirical constraint satisfaction.

title: A thorough review on Deep Learning approaches to 2D-to-3D Registration in Medical Imaging
summary: 2D-to-3D image registration is a key component for several medical imaging purposes such as intraoperative guidance, enabling the alignment between preoperative 3D volumes and real-time 2D images. While conventional optimisation-based methods often struggle with non-convex objectives, sensitivity to initialisation, and high computational demands, deep learning (DL) has emerged as a promising alternative, offering improved alignment robustness and the potential for real-time performance. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of DL frameworks developed to address the challenges inherent in 2D-to-3D registration. We first outline how core concepts of DL are adapted to the registration problem. We then examine recent methodological advancements from multiple perspectives, including pipeline design, architectural innovations, and domain adaptation strategies. Particular attention is given to quantitative metrics, highlighting how performance is defined and measured across studies. Across the 41 included studies, we find that direct regression is the most common pipeline (23 studies, against 18 iterative ones), that hybrid CNN-attention architectures are gaining ground, and that research remains heavily concentrated on X-ray-to-CT registration. We conclude by identifying the absence of per-case uncertainty estimation and the strong neglect of temporal or sequential modelling as the two methodological gaps most consequential for clinical readiness, and discuss state-space models as a way to add temporal memory within intraoperative latency budgets. Further opportunities lie in more principled domain adaptation and in the integration of foundation models for representation learning.

title: RAZeR: Representation Aware Zonotope Reduction
summary: Reachability analysis is a popular technique for verifying the safety of a dynamical system under uncertainty, where the uncertainty is often represented by zonotopes. As the size of the zonotope representation typically grows as the reachability analysis progresses, it must be repeatedly reduced at the cost of additional conservatism. While various methods exist to reduce the size of the representation, combined advantages are not fully leveraged as only a single reduction method is typically used throughout the analysis. In this work, we show how dynamically choosing which method to use can yield significantly tighter results, thereby easing verification. This is realized by introducing a heuristic, derived from model predictive control, that accounts for upcoming propagation of the current zonotope. We argue that order reduction is not merely a post-processing step after propagation but also a pre-processing step that shapes how the zonotope evolves under the system dynamics. We evaluate our approach, RAZeR, on nonlinear benchmarks taken from the ARCH-COMP, where we demonstrate that RAZeR produces tighter zonotopes at a negligible performance overhead.

title: Enumerating Posterior-Supported Priors: First-Order Error of Finite-Integral Cross-Categorical Measurement Morphisms
summary: In generative modeling, standard measure theory adopts the a.e. convention, which legitimately ignores any error component carried by a null-support set: a single null element can hide out-of-domain error inside null support and never be explicitly accounted for. The contribution of this paper is not a new distributional distance, but rather a verifiable structure that writes down which underlying predicate supports a high-level object, when it is invertible, and at which layer the error resides, from which we propose the enumerating posterior-supported prior framework. The framework operates on a three-layer categorical chain Quot->MorTop->Set: the first two layers posit no point elements and take binary-predicate quotient partitions as objects; the replica-index counting measure successively discriminates one-to-many collections into injections, lifting object collection from surjection to a quotient-layer bijection; the mutual exclusion of preimages in the shared measure space is resolved by an invertible MPT. Four results consolidate into Thm. 7: binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects support the set categorical functional along categorical support via measure descent--recovery, enumerating the morphism itself rather than its preimage and object; their multiplicity is normalized through replica-index injection and accounted as an explicitly first-order error. The contribution of this paper is a transformation from nontrivial-input construction -> engineering-computable first-order output: the binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects, supported via categorical support measure descent--recovery, constitute a substantive nontrivial input---precisely because they lift the out-of-domain error that hid inside null support into a first-order falsifiable coefficient mu_err, a finitely obtainable finite integral first-order error.

title: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors
summary: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.

title: Learning monotone game-theoretic linear MPC
summary: We propose a method to learn a game-theoretic model predictive control (GT-MPC) law by imitation from input and output data of a running multi-agent system. By interpreting the recorded inputs as the first moves of the equilibria of a game played by the agents, we learn the GT-MPC weights under hard input constraints and soft output constraints, without requiring the agents to reveal their objectives. We also impose that the resulting generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problem is strongly monotone, which ensures the existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium and, hence, that the learned GT-MPC law is well defined and can be evaluated efficiently online by variational GNE-seeking algorithms for linear-quadratic games. Moreover, strong monotonicity implies that the equilibrium is almost everywhere differentiable with respect to the references and the weights, which enables automatic differentiation for gradient-based optimization. In addition, we promote closed-loop stability of the unconstrained equilibrium feedback by incorporating a penalty that involves a jointly learned quadratic Lyapunov function. Learning a GT-MPC formulation enables us to explain the agents' objectives, reproduce their behavior in simulation in new scenarios, optimize their set-points, design mechanisms, and enforce additional constraints. A numerical example illustrates the approach.

title: Envelope Model for GTEx Data
summary: This article studies the envelope model for enhanced gene expression analysis using GTEx data. The study compares this advanced statistical approach with standard multivariate linear regression, demonstrating improved capacity for identifying significant genes and enhanced estimation efficiency. By partitioning response variation into material and immaterial components, the envelope model reduces estimation noise, leading to stronger statistical signals and smaller standard errors. These findings, as demonstrated in our tissue-specific and gene-group anal- yses, show that the envelope model can pick up on important biological signals that traditional methods tend to miss. This makes it a useful tool for genomic studies and GTEx data analysis.

title: Does the Ranking Hold? A Practitioner-Facing Audit of Hallucination Detectors on Small, Quantized, On-Device LLMs
summary: Hallucination detection for large language models is dominated by methods evaluated on 7B-70B research models with abundant sampling budgets and exact-match or ROUGE correctness labels. The small models practitioners actually ship on-device, Phi-3-mini, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-Instruct, typically at 4-bit precision, sit outside this evidence base. We present a reproducible one-GPU audit of four detectors spanning three paradigms: length-normalized token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, and two sampling-based consistency methods (semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI) on two small open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit NF4 quantization on a single Colab T4 GPU, evaluated on closed-book TriviaQA. Cross-model ranking transfer is poor: Spearman rho is -0.80 and Kendall tau-b is -0.667, meaning the detector ranking actively inverts between the two models, and the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from the sampling-based consistency detectors on both models under bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals. As a second, methodological contribution, we show that the standard token-overlap-to-multiple-choice correctness labeler for TruthfulQA-Generation produces near-chance AUROC (0.46-0.59) for all four detectors on both models, a labeler failure, not a detector failure, since the same detectors reach 0.69-0.89 AUROC on TriviaQA under the identical pipeline. We release the harness, prompts, and per-item scores and frame the detector choice explicitly as a fairness-of-error-rates allocation problem for practitioners deploying on resource-constrained, on-device hardware.

title: Sub-Synchronous Control Interaction Risk of Large Data Center Loads: A Frequency-Scan Assessment with Cross-Model Validation
comment: 13 pages, 16 figures. Submitted for IEEE publications
summary: Data centers are now one of the fastest-growing loads on the bulk power system, and most of their demand reaches the grid through power converters inside uninterruptible power supplies (UPS). Whether these loads can take part in sub-synchronous control interaction (SSCI), as wind and HVDC converters do, has not been studied extensively. We examine this question with impedance-based frequency scans at the point of common coupling (PCC). Using a detailed proprietary model (INS-ISU), we scan the motor, variable-frequency-drive (VFD), lighting, and UPS-fed information-technology (IT) branches of a representative facility separately. Only the UPS in double-conversion mode shows negative resistance; it covers the whole sub-synchronous band and continues up to about 170 Hz. The other branches, and the UPS in bypass mode, stay passive. We then repeat the scans on three public models from PNNL, TAMU, and NLR. None of them shows negative resistance in bypass mode, while three of the four models do in double-conversion mode. Lowering the load from rated to light load makes the negative resistance deeper, as expected for a constant-power load, so a lightly loaded facility in double-conversion mode is the worst case. Raising the UPS DC-link capacitance pushes the negative resistance into a narrow band around the fundamental. These findings give a basis for screening data centers for SSCI during interconnection studies.

title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Dynamical Systems
comment: 19 pages, AIAA SciTech Forum 2027 (Uncertainty Quantification Conference)
summary: This paper presents a multifidelity (MF) formulation of Operator Inference (OpInf) for learning non-intrusive, physics-based reduced-order models (ROMs) of nonlinear dynamical systems. OpInf learns reduced operators from projections of snapshot data by solving a least squares regression problem. However, generating high-fidelity snapshots can be computationally expensive, limiting parameter coverage and the temporal extent of training trajectories for many aerospace applications, which can lead to inaccurate or unstable ROM predictions. This work proposes MF-OpInf, which combines limited high-fidelity snapshots with more plentiful low-fidelity snapshots through a control-variates-inspired MF least squares formulation to learn a single set of reduced operators across multiple trajectories. Low-fidelity trajectories provide additional parameter coverage and extend beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. The low-fidelity snapshots are also used to construct an improved reduced basis through weighted proper orthogonal decomposition. We demonstrate MF-OpInf on a nonlinear reaction-diffusion problem with parametrized sinusoidal forcing and a two-dimensional incompressible flow past a cylinder with a parametrized inlet pulse. In these experiments, under an equal training simulation budget, MF-OpInf reduces the mean relative prediction error at unseen parameters by up to $87\%$ for the reaction-diffusion problem and $28\%$ for the cylinder flow problem over the test time regime, which extends beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. These results demonstrate that MF-OpInf can improve temporal extrapolation and prediction at unseen parameters without increasing the training simulation budget.

title: LoRAWeaver: Directional Adapter Routing in LoRA Representation Space
summary: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters. This pool complicates adapter selection during inference. Existing routing and encoder-based methods often require retraining when new adapters are added, which limits their use in dynamic settings. This paper treats adapter routing as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The proposed training-free method selects adapters by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and on out-of-distribution tasks show that the method outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder without learning a router. An ablation confirms the benefit of directional alignment in the adapter-output space.

title: Battery Energy Storage Sizing in PV Ramp-Rate Smoothing using Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Based Controller
summary: This paper presents a constraint-aware reinforcement learning (CARL) controller for battery energy storage system (BESS) sizing and photovoltaic (PV) ramp-rate smoothing. Rapid PV power fluctuations caused by cloud transitions can introduce operational and stability challenges in power systems. To mitigate these impacts, grid codes impose ramp-rate limits (RRL) on PV power injected to the grid. BESSs can support such grid codes by absorbing or supplying power during rapid variations. However, the extent to which BESSs can reduce PV-induced variability depends on (i) the BESS power and energy capacities; and (ii) the adopted controller. Thus, BESS sizing and controller design are coupled. Conventional moving-average control can increase battery usage due to filter-induced lag, while ramp-rate control is reactive and does not account for the long-term impact of actions on battery state of charge and future ramp events. Optimization-based methods can reduce BESS requirements by anticipating future PV variations, but their performance depends on accurate PV forecasts. To address these limitations, the CARL controller learns a causal state-feedback policy from historical PV data without requiring forecasts during deployment. Ramp-rate, converter-power, and state-of-charge constraints are incorporated into a causal feasibility interval that guarantees feasible actions by definition. A full-horizon input-convex neural network (ICNN)-based optimization is developed as a noncausal benchmark for the minimum achievable BESS requirements. Evaluation using three real-world PV datasets shows that, at a 10\%/min ramp-rate limit, CARL reduces peak BESS power by 8.7--10.4\% and energy capacity by 47.5--62.6\% relative to conventional ramp-rate control while maintaining the grid-codes compliance.

title: Parametric Modal SARIMA Models with Skewed Distributions
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Supplementary tables and figures are provided as an ancillary file
summary: Seasonal autoregressive integrated moving-average (SARIMA) models typically target the conditional mean of a time series under a Gaussian error assumption. This approach may be inadequate when the innovations are asymmetric because the conditional mean no longer represents the most likely outcome. We propose the Modal SARIMA$(p,d,q)\times(P,D,Q)_s$ model, which links the conditional mode, rather than the conditional mean, to a multiplicative seasonal ARIMA structure. The innovations follow the Fernandez-Steel class of skewed distributions (SKD), whose location parameter is the mode, and the non-seasonal Modal ARIMA$(p,d,q)$ model is the special case without seasonal terms. We give the conditional log-likelihood for the Skew-Normal, Skewed Student-$t$, and Skewed Laplace members, establish the stationarity and invertibility conditions on the product polynomials, show that the recursive modal forecast is the joint mode of the future trajectory, and characterize the correction that yields the marginal $h$-step conditional mode. Monte Carlo experiments show that conditional maximum likelihood and its Wald inference are reliable when the seasonal factors are well separated, that the test of symmetry holds its level from about 200 observations, and that the modal estimator of the dynamic coefficients is as efficient as Gaussian least squares under symmetry and 1.2 to 2.6 times more efficient under asymmetry or heavy tails. We also show, analytically and by simulation, that nearly cancelling seasonal factors amplify the effect of the starting values, and that beyond one step the recursive forecast must be corrected to remain a forecast of the most probable value. In an application to the Canadian lynx trappings, a seasonal component for the ten-year cycle improves the non-seasonal fit for every member of the SKD family. The methods are implemented in the R package ModalForecast.

title: Tabular Population Priors as Structured Retrieval for EHR Medication Set Prediction
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Structured Data for Health (SD4H), Seoul, South Korea
summary: Medication prediction from electronic health records is a fixed vocabulary structured prediction problem, yet recent clinical RAG systems often treat it like open ended case based reasoning: retrieve similar patient admissions and ask an LLM to infer a medication set. This retrieval object is indirect the model receives retrieved patient records while the target is a discrete set of medication class labels. We propose a more task aligned retrieval object: a tabular population prior ranked medication class candidates from a sparse condition medication co occurrence table estimated from training admissions. Using PACERAG as a fixed downstream pipeline and replacing only its patient retriever, this drop in swap improves F1 from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 on 1,004 heldout MIMIC IV admissions, with no additional LLM calls and no inference time patient index. A non LLM top k baseline reaches F1=0.248, confirming the prior is predictive before LLM integration. Aggregate population statistics can provide a more task aligned, efficient, and auditable retrieval source than patient level nearest neighbors for fixed vocabulary EHR set prediction.

title: When to Move: Online Repositioning of Movable Antenna Arrays Under a Long-Term Actuation Energy Budget
summary: Movable antenna (MA) arrays improve multiuser throughput by repositioning their elements, but mechanical movement reduces transmission time and consumes actuation energy. Changes in user configurations create nonuniform demand for repositioning over time, while each movement determines which positions are reachable in subsequent slots. Thus, online control must decide when to spend a limited actuation-energy budget, not only where to position the antennas. We formulate causal effective-throughput maximization under displacement-dependent movement delay, inter-slot reachability, and a long-term average actuation-energy constraint. We propose Lyapunov-based online movable-antenna repositioning (LOMA), which adjusts the price of movement through a virtual queue and solves the resulting nonconvex position problem via proximal minorization--maximization, accounting for nonsmooth movement delay and promoting sparse antenna updates. We establish monotone ascent of the smoothed per-slot objective, a finite-horizon sample-path energy bound, almost-sure long-term budget feasibility under a Gaussian fading model with bounded large-scale gains, and a state-matched throughput comparison separating temporal energy allocation from per-slot optimization error. Simulations show that LOMA concentrates actuation after intermittent user changes and improves effective throughput over optimized fixed arrays and a per-slot-budget counterpart, while continuous channel drift favors more frequent incremental repositioning. Additional simulations with pilot-based channel estimates in sparse millimeter-wave channels show that LOMA retains most of the throughput benefits of online repositioning while operating near its prescribed long-term actuation-energy budget.

title: Bayesian Semiparametric Regression for Count Data Using Zero Altered Moment Models
summary: We develop a Bayesian semiparametric regression framework for count data that can accommodate both underdispersion and overdispersion without specifying a full parametric probability model. The model is built from the first two conditional factorial moments of a zero altered distribution. Covariates may enter the conditional mean and the conditional dispersion separately, thereby allowing the dispersion to vary across observations. We turn the moment restrictions into an adjusted exponentially tilted empirical likelihood (AETEL) criterion and combine this criterion with Gaussian priors to form a Bayesian empirical-likelihood pseudo-posterior. The adjustment improves numerical feasibility and a two-block Metropolis delayed acceptance sampler allows for faster runs of the MCMC chains. This reduces unnecessary exact evaluations without changing the AETEL target. Using existing Bayesian exponentially tilted empirical likelihood (ETEL) theory, we state a first-order posterior normal approximation and verify the moment, smoothness, and Jacobian rank conditions needed for the asymptotic inference. Simulations under zero inflated Poisson and Conway Maxwell Poisson data exhibit small bias, accurate uncertainty estimates, and near nominal interval coverage for both overdispersed and underdispersed counts. Applications to various datasets illustrate how the Bayesian analysis can identify covariate dependent dispersion using finite sample posterior inference.

title: Everything is an Operational View: UI as a Projection over Context in Agentic Systems
summary: The emergence of generative AI has enabled Generative User Interfaces (GenUI) that dynamically construct interfaces from user intent, yet existing approaches rely on request-response pipelines that fragment context and limit transparency and control. This paper proposes AFS-UI, which reconceptualises UI as projections over context built on an agentic file-system abstraction that organizes data, capabilities, and interaction state within a unified, persistent workspace. In particular, AFS-UI addresses key limitations in current systems, including heterogeneous resource discoverability, incompatible operation semantics, tangling projection and context, rigid source composition and substitution, and limited evolvability. Within this framework, interfaces become dynamic, inspectable views over shared resources, supporting both human and agent interaction through a common operational surface.

title: Feasibility of Pareto-Improving Damping Control of Forced Oscillations: The Active-Power Case
summary: Damping control of a forced oscillation may reduce amplitudes at certain locations while increasing them elsewhere. This paper introduces Pareto improvement as a criterion for assessing such control: at least one nodal oscillation amplitude decreases, while none increases across all other nodes. The analysis considers active-power forcing sources and active-power control injections in connected swing networks with positive inertia and damping. Necessary conditions for Pareto improvement feasibility are derived from the normalized nodal responses. It is proven that for every network with a single oscillation source and a single actuator, at least one positive forcing frequency is shown to preclude Pareto improvement, regardless of the amplitude and phase of the control input. A three-node counterexample shows that this limitation does not persist with multiple actuators. PSS/E simulations of a 6-bus benchmark system and a modified IEEE 39-bus system validated the analysis. These findings suggest the value of assessing control effects across the network and further investigating multi-actuator damping control.

title: A Spatial Analysis of Proximity to the Built Environment and Wildfire Ignition Cause in the United States
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures. Under review at the International Journal of Wildland Fire
summary: Background. Human activities in areas with burnable land cover can lead to wildfire ignitions, and higher levels of human presence increase the likelihood of such fires. Building locations provide a widely available representation of human presence. Aims. This study examines how accurately proximity to buildings predicts wildfire ignition cause across different land-cover types. Methods. Supervised classification methods were applied to building, land-cover, and ignition data for the contiguous United States to estimate the conditional probability that an ignition is human-caused. Proximity to buildings was represented using either building density within surrounding zones or distance to nearby areas with high building density. Key results. Both methods, particularly the distance-based approach, showed that proximity to buildings is a strong predictor of ignition cause: approximately three quarters of both human- and lightning-caused ignitions were correctly classified. Retraining the models separately for individual states did not substantially improve classification performance relative to the national model. Conclusions. Building proximity is an effective predictor of wildfire ignition cause, and the relationship between ignition cause and building-related predictors is similar across many regions of the contiguous United States. Implications. Building-proximity variables can be incorporated into wildfire forecasting and risk assessment models to improve prediction of human-caused wildfire ignitions.

title: fieldsmith: Automated symbolic derivation in classical field theory and gauge theory from LaTeX input
summary: We present fieldsmith, an open-source Python library for the automated derivation of analytical results in classical field theory, and non-abelian gauge theories. A Lagrangian is entered the way it is written on a blackboard, in LaTeX index notation, and the library produces and verifies Euler-Lagrange equations (of arbitrary derivative order, on flat or curved backgrounds), Noether currents and identities, canonical and Hilbert energy-momentum tensors, canonical momenta and Hamiltonians, local Poisson brackets and a Dirac-Bergmann constraint analysis with degree-of-freedom counting, linearised wave equations and dispersion relations, gauge-covariant derivatives and field strengths for products of unitary groups, and mass spectra after spontaneous symmetry breaking. A fitting routine translates component-level output back into covariant index notation, and a grading module checks students' submitted field equations, identities and conserved currents. The implementation is a compact (about 2,700 lines) layer on top of SymPy: tensors are stored by components with labelled, variance-aware slots, and every statement is established by exact symbolic computation rather than pattern matching. This document is the companion guide to the library. It explains the intent and design, describes the algorithms, and then works through eighteen self-checking examples, ranging from the Klein-Gordon field to the BPST instanton and the 't Hooft-Polyakov monopole, each preceded by the background physics needed to follow it. The examples double as a compact introduction to classical field theory and gauge theory as seen through a computational lens. We are explicit about the limitations of the approach.

title: Brain-inspired Beam Selection for mmWave RIS Communication
summary: Beam selection at large passive reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) requires either full channel knowledge or beam training, both of which entail unwanted overhead. On the other hand, learned models that predict the optimal codeword from channels sampled at a few active elements avoid both, at the cost of energy-demanding multiply-and-accumulate operations. In this paper, we propose spiking neural network (SNN)-based beam selection for a semi-active RIS assisting a mmWave multiple-input single-output communication system. Direct and sigmoid rate coding are compared against a multi- layer perceptron (MLP) of identical architecture. Energy analysis further reveals that the input layer dominates SNN energy consumption.

title: Regularized parametric modal regression for positive responses with high-dimensional covariates
comment: 15 pages, 7 tables. R package ModalNet: https://github.com/chedgala/ModalNet
summary: Modal regression models the conditional mode rather than the conditional mean, which is attractive for positive and right-skewed responses whose mean is distorted by the upper tail. We propose a regularized version of parametric modal regression for positive responses with high-dimensional covariates, in which the density parameters of the Gamma, Weibull and Lognormal distributions are written as functions of the conditional mode and the log-likelihood is penalized by the Lasso, adaptive Lasso or elastic-net penalties. The estimates are computed by a proximal Newton algorithm, equivalently an iteratively reweighted penalized least-squares scheme, whose inner problem is solved exactly by the coordinate-descent routines of glmnet, and the regularization parameter is selected by the extended Bayesian information criterion. We show that the Lognormal estimator coincides with the Gaussian Lasso applied to the log-transformed response, that under constant dispersion the conditional mean and the conditional mode have the same slopes, and that the estimation error attains the rate $O(\sqrt{s}λ_n)$ with no smoothing bias. Simulation studies with up to $p = 1000$ covariates show that the method improves on the Lasso applied to the log-transformed response for Gamma and Weibull responses, and two applications illustrate its use. The method is implemented in the R package ModalNet.

title: Beyond Attack-Based Accuracy: Rethinking Adversarial Robustness Evaluation Through Structural Gradient Alignment
summary: Visual adversarial robustness remains a fundamental security property as vision systems evolve from conventional classifiers to vision-language models (VLMs) and large vision-language models (LVLMs), with visual inputs remaining an attack surface across generations. Yet existing evaluation methods often depend on prescribed attacks, in-distribution data, extensive probing, or classifier-specific formulations, limiting external auditing of diverse models. We introduce Structural Gradient Alignment (SGA), a complementary robustness metric measuring the structural alignment between input content and objective-conditioned local model sensitivity. SGA uses a few randomly sampled, unlabeled public probes that need not follow the downstream task distribution and only one input-gradient computation per model--probe pair. Across 38 distinct DNNs, VLMs, and LVLMs, SGA produces rankings consistent with attack-based references. Without robustness references, uncalibrated SGA achieves $83.72\%$ average pairwise agreement across eight public-probe conditions, outperforming the strongest overall baseline in all eight by $9.38$ percentage points on average. With known robustness orders of anchor models, calibrated SGA increases agreement to $85.36\%$. These results demonstrate an attack-agnostic, computationally efficient robustness signal across conventional DNNs, VLMs, and autoregressive LVLMs, downstream tasks, threat norms, probe distributions, and evaluator-knowledge settings. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/azrealwang/SGA.

title: Efficient Design of Flag Sequence Sets for Delay-Doppler Estimation via Riemannian Optimization
summary: This letter investigates the design of a Flag sequence set with peak-curtain auto-ambiguity functions to enable low-complexity delay-Doppler estimation. Given the predefined Curtain sequences, the Flag sequence set design problem is formulated as the minimization of the weighted integrated masked sidelobe level. To solve this problem, we first reformulate it as an unconstrained optimization problem on the unimodular manifold. Then, a tailored unimodular manifold conjugate gradient (UM-CG) algorithm is developed. Compared with the existing define algorithm, the proposed UM-CG algorithm reduces computational and storage requirements. Moreover, the global convergence of the proposed UM-CG scheme is theoretically derived under mild conditions. Numerical results demonstrate the superior optimization performance of the proposed UM-CG algorithm and show that the designed Flag sequences exhibit nearly ideal peak-curtain properties.

title: Identifiability and Spectral Estimation of Mixed Memberships in Heterogeneous Multilayer Networks
summary: Multilayer network data, arising from multiple sources, repeated measurements, or multi-view interactions, are increasingly common, highlighting the need for statistical methods that jointly leverage information across layers while allowing for layer heterogeneity and computational scalability. Here, we study a multilayer degree-corrected mixed membership model (ML-DCMM), in which nodes share a common mixed membership across layers while degree effects and block connectivity patterns vary by layer. This model encompasses several existing models for multilayer data while preserving identifiability and interpretation. We develop a spectral estimation procedure that integrates layer-wise embeddings with corner estimation for membership recovery. A further refinement that connects the resulting representation to a ParaTuck-2 tensor decomposition is also introduced. We establish theoretical guarantees for the proposed spectral method, showing that the probability of near-corner recovery increases with the number of layers, and we provide the convergence rate for the resulting membership estimator. We establish a minimax lower bound for membership estimation, which does not improve with increasing number of layers. Simulation studies show that ML-DCMM can outperform other approaches under strong layer heterogeneity. In an analysis of London bike-sharing networks, the methodology recovers interpretable memberships and achieves lower held-out edge prediction error under edge-sampling cross-validation than competing models.

title: ProdPilot: A Layered Model Context Protocol System for Automated Production Readiness and Deployment of Vibe-Coded Projects
summary: AI-assisted development environments turn natural-language requests into working applications, yet the projects they produce often fail on their first deployment for operational reasons: credentials in source files, missing security middleware, no container definition, no health endpoint and no delivery pipeline. Automated repair of such defects usually relies on free-form model generation, which varies between runs and is seldom checked independently. This paper presents ProdPilot, a local Model Context Protocol server that audits Node.js and React projects against 50 production readiness rules, repairs violations through a bounded loop, gates the result and deploys it. Each rule is classified by what its fix requires: 28 fixes are fixed templates, 16 are filled with values extracted from the project and only 6 are written by the IDE agent's model, so 88.0\% of the ruleset needs no model-written content, and across 499 real repositories 93.5\% of the violations found fall in those classes. A fix, however it was produced, is accepted only if the checker that flagged the rule now passes. In a full-chain run over 23 sample projects, template and extraction fixes that were applied as written passed their checkers in 87.6\% and 95.0\% of cases, and independent verification rejected 25 of the 237 fixes reported as applied. A deployability model trained on 684 real deployments ranks held-out projects at 0.909 ROC AUC, a gated project was deployed, smoke-tested and connected to an active CI/CD pipeline in 82 seconds, and the unchanged server worked from the IDE agents in VS Code, Cursor and Windsurf, where live agents resolved all six delegated rules on the first attempt under the same verification. ProdPilot itself runs no model.

title: Orbit-AWARE: From Onboard AI Deployment to Sustainable In-Orbit Intelligence
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables, submitted to IEEE Wireless Communications
summary: The growing role of space computing in time-critical satellite services makes the long-term reliability of onboard artificial intelligence (AI) a mission-level requirement. Model drift can undermine this reliability through critical-observation suppression or noncritical priority flooding, displacing both mission information and evidence for model correction. To address this drift-induced evidence displacement, this article presents Orbit-AWARE, a safeguard-first lifecycle management (LCM) architecture. A comparison of existing approaches motivates cooperative Data, Cognitive, and Trust Planes for continuous monitoring, event-triggered agentic orchestration, and deterministic governance. The architecture retains a model-independent sample stream before degradation is confirmed and coordinates evidence selection and exchange for diagnosis and ground-assisted adaptation. Candidate updates are verified before control over data disposition is restored. In an xBD-based emergency Earth observation (EO) case study, Orbit-AWARE delivers 14.3\% more critical observations and achieves 8.3\% higher sustainable mission utility than the Rule-Based Drift Loop under a common 10\% downlink budget. Finally, we discuss future research directions for extending LCM through task-aware reliability assessment, memory- and tool-enabled onboard agents, and evidence-centric space networking. This work makes evidence availability and recovery authorization explicit design objectives for dependable onboard AI services.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Continual Learning for 2D XRD Interpretation Using Simulated and Experimental Data
summary: Autonomous experimentation systems require characterization models that can interpret heterogeneous measurements and maintain predictive performance as data accumulate. Developing such models involves addressing domain mismatch between data sources, overconfident predictions on unfamiliar inputs, and catastrophic forgetting during sequential updates. In this work, we present a proof-of-concept framework for uncertainty-aware continual interpretation of two-dimensional X-ray diffraction (XRD) data. The framework integrates established components: maximum mean discrepancy-based domain adaptation to reduce simulation-to-experiment discrepancies, a convolutional neural network with a spectral-normalized neural Gaussian process (CNN--SNGP) for predictive uncertainty estimation, and replay with knowledge distillation for sequential model updating. We evaluate the framework using simulated and previously-collected experimental data for crystal structure classification of single-phase body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonal close-packed patterns. Data are organized into predefined sequential blocks to assess adaptation and retention of previously learned knowledge. Within this setting, the results show accurate classification across simulated and experimental data, improved alignment between the two domains, and reduced forgetting compared with naïve fine-tuning. Predictive uncertainty is also evaluated on unfamiliar and noisy inputs. The contribution is the integration and evaluation of these capabilities for sequential XRD interpretation. The framework provides a basis for future integration into autonomous experimentation systems, with experimental planning, instrument control, and closed-loop deployment remaining areas for future development.

title: TSP instances that require exponentially many subtour elimination constraints
summary: We construct pathological TSP instances that require exponentially many subtour elimination constraints (SECs) in the sense that, if a smaller collection of SECs is imposed, then the Dantzig-Fulkerson-Johnson model returns a disconnected solution costing less than an optimal tour. For asymmetric instances on $n$ vertices, we prove a growth rate of \(Ω(φ^n)\), where \(φ\approx 1.618\) is the golden ratio. A node-splitting reduction gives metric instances with \(Ω(φ^{n/2})\) growth. We also give instances in the plane under the Euclidean, Rectilinear, and Maximum metrics that require exponentially many SECs. Concorde struggles on them, with solve times growing exponentially despite tiny integrality gaps.

title: Frequency-Security-Aware Real-Time Economic Dispatch with Data Center UPS Flexibility for Inertia and Primary Frequency Response Services
summary: The increasing penetration of renewable energy and the rapid growth of AI data centers are introducing significant challenges to power system frequency security. There is an urgent need to identify grid-compatible resources capable of providing fast frequency support. This paper proposes a frequency-security-aware real-time economic dispatch (RTED) model that enables data center (DC) uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems to provide steady-state power balancing, inertia response, and primary frequency response (PFR) services. Specifically, tractable analytical frequency-security constraints are derived and incorporated into the RTED framework through second-order cone programming (SOCP) formulation. The proposed model jointly optimizes energy, reserve, and inertia to minimize system operation cost while preventing under-frequency load shedding (UFLS). Numerical validation on a modified IEEE 39-bus system demonstrates that the proposed RTED model with UPS flexibility can economically support system operation and significantly improve frequency security under active-power deficit disturbances.

title: Homogeneous pursuit in $β$ model
summary: Data in forms of networks has been encountered in various prevalent fields at the arrival of big data era. To unveil and recover the true model with core units with numerous links, the $β$-model under sparsity constraint is proposed to meet the expectation of statisticians and engineers. Not only does this network model inherit spectacular property from the Erdős-Rényi model, but also exhibits degree heterogeneity through tuning sparsity parameter $s$. In this paper, we propose Homogeneous Pursuit (HP), an $\ell_0$-constrained maximum likelihood estimation method implemented through a primal-dual algorithm. To ease the harshness of computation, we find the surrogate function of the corresponding objective function to derive Majorization Minimization algorithm through the primal-dual process. Moreover, after meticulous evaluation, the algorithm brought about captures the property of fine convergence rate in a contraction mapping way. Under some mild conditions, the proposed generalized information criterion (GIC$^*$) for selecting the sparsity level is consistent to find the truth. Combining HP with GIC$^*$ gives the adaptive procedure HP-GIC$^*$; HP-BIC denotes the same estimation method with sparsity selected by BIC. Finally, simulation studies show that GIC$^*$ improves support recovery relative to BIC in the reported comparisons, while HP achieves lower computational cost while maintaining estimation accuracy comparable to the sparse benchmark methods. A microfinance application illustrates the use of HP-GIC$^*$ for studying the association between network prominence and participation, with improved fit in the reported village-level regressions.

title: Time-Consistent Evaluation of Hierarchical Code Graphs for SWE Agents
summary:
Evaluating repository-aware software engineering (SWE) agents requires strict separation between pre-existing repository knowledge and future code evolution, yet standard benchmarks frequently suffer from temporal contamination and prompt-level solution leakage. Building on the time-consistent benchmark protocol of Sun (2026), we enforce strict zero-leakage isolation across DragonFly in C++ and React in JavaScript/TypeScript, locking repository snapshots and knowledge graphs at historical cutoff commits $T_0$ and evaluating 100 post-$T_0$ pull requests across four prompt granularities: Minimal, Concise, Contextual, and Guided.
  Under this zero-leakage protocol, we conduct a matched evaluation of three context-augmentation regimes: (1) an unaugmented Baseline, (2) a flat syntax-level Tree-sitter AST graph, and (3) ServiceExplorer, a deterministic two-level hierarchical dependency graph capturing Level-1 system/package containers and Level-2 architectural modules. Across 7,200 paired evaluations spanning six foundation models across the MAI-Code Flash, Claude, and GPT-Sol families, ServiceExplorer consistently outperforms both Baseline and Tree-sitter AST across every model, repository, and prompt granularity ($+15.6\%$ to $+86.2\%$ relative $F_1$ lift, $p < 10^{-4}$), while tripling exact full-PR localization on DragonFly. Crucially, equipping an efficiency-tier or prior-generation model with ServiceExplorer consistently surpasses the unaugmented Baseline $F_1$ of the next-generation model across all evaluated families.

title: A Tumour-Aware Multimodal Framework for Explainable Prediction of IDH Mutation in Gliomas from Multi-Sequence MRI
comment: 45 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Preprint of an article submitted for consideration in International Journal of Information Technology & Decision Making (World Scientific)
summary: Accurate prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status is essential for glioma diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. Although recent deep learning approaches have demonstrated promising performance, many rely on whole-brain feature extraction and provide limited interpretability. This study proposes a tumour-aware multimodal framework for explainable, non-invasive prediction of IDH mutation status from multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The proposed framework integrates four MRI sequences (T1, T1CE, T2, and FLAIR), tumour subregion segmentation, quantitative radiomic descriptors, and clinical information within a unified deep learning architecture. An ablation study was conducted to evaluate the contribution of tumour-aware learning, radiomic features, and clinical variables. Model performance was assessed using multiple complementary evaluation metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, balanced accuracy, receiver operating characteristic analysis, confusion matrix evaluation, and Grad-CAM visualisation. Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed multimodal framework consistently outperformed the baseline MRI-only model, with the Clinical Fusion model achieving the strongest overall predictive performance. The integration of tumour-aware learning, radiomic descriptors, and clinical information progressively improved classification performance, while Grad-CAM visualisations indicated that the model predominantly focused on biologically relevant tumour regions. These findings suggest that tumour-aware multimodal feature integration enables accurate, interpretable, and non-invasive molecular profiling of gliomas and provides a promising foundation for future clinical decision support in precision neuro-oncology.

title: GIC model selection for high-dimensional CCA
summary: Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) is a widely used statistical tool for exploring the dependence structure between two sets of variables. An important issue in CCA is determining the rank. Among information-based criteria for rank selection, the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) are two commonly used approaches. Both rely on the number of free parameters to quantify model complexity, which may not adequately account for the underlying dependence structure when the assumed model is misspecified. As a result, AIC and BIC may exhibit unsatisfactory performance, particularly when the remaining canonical correlations do not follow the assumed low-dimensional structure. To alleviate this difficulty, we adopt the idea of the generalized information criterion (GIC) to develop a data-adaptive measure of model complexity for CCA rank selection. The proposed complexity measure incorporates the magnitudes of the sample canonical correlations, thereby accounting for the spectral structure of the data and improving robustness to model misspecification. We investigate the asymptotic properties of the proposed GIC under a high-dimensional setting in which the sample size and both variable dimensions grow proportionally. Our theoretical analysis aims to characterize the conditions under which GIC can distinguish signal canonical correlations from noise and achieve more reliable rank selection than conventional information criteria.

title: Evolutionary-based Transfer Learning for Physical Attack on End-to-End Autoencoder Communications
comment: 31 pages, 10 figures, and 4 tables. Accepted by JNCA
summary: End-to-end autoencoder communication has emerged as a promising means of achieving efficient data transmission across various domains. Nevertheless, vulnerabilities have recently been revealed in these systems by adversarial attacks, wherein malevolent entities manipulate the transmitted signals to deceive the autoencoder. This paper leverages the applications of evolutionary algorithms to solve a challenging optimization problem of launching physical attacks against end-to-end autoencoder communication. For white-box scenarios, we introduce PAGA (Physical Attack based on Genetic Algorithm), which combines a genetic algorithm with elite population initialization to craft attack signals that degrade autoencoder performance. To gauge the efficacy of these attack signals, we employ a fitness function that assesses their capacity to induce substantial reconstruction errors and misclassification rates. A Multi-Factorial version of PAGA, referred to as PAMFGA, is proposed to deal with practical scenarios where the attackers have limited knowledge about the receiver, also known as a black-box attack. Our experimental results show that the proposed attacks can substantially degrade the reliability of the considered autoencoder communication systems across the evaluated settings. This study also underscores the critical importance of incorporating security considerations into the design and implementation of end-to-end autoencoder communication systems.

title: State-of-Charge Targets for Storage Participation in Two-Settlement Markets: Reliability, Price, and Compensation Impacts
summary: As energy storage assumes a larger role in electricity systems, market operation must coordinate its use across time to support reliability during periods of system stress. Minimum state-of-charge (SOC) targets provide a means of preserving energy for these periods, but their design shapes reliability, operating efficiency, and storage compensation. This paper evaluates alternative SOC target designs in a California-based day-ahead and real-time electricity market model. The comparison examines targets based on day-ahead schedules or rolling centralized dispatch, enforced at the individual-resource or system level, across seasons, stress conditions, and participant information settings. The results show that retaining more energy does not necessarily reduce load shedding: targets that restrict discharge can limit storage support during shortages. Under critical summer conditions, individual targets derived from rolling centralized dispatch reduce weekly load shedding by approximately 83--84\% relative to operation without targets. Lower RT clearing costs and average prices can coexist with higher storage compensation, reflecting the role of day-ahead positions and real-time deviations in determining settlement outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of coordinating energy retention with timely discharge and network deliverability when designing SOC requirements for storage participation in electricity markets.

title: Minimaxity in Robust Nonparametric Regression: from Heavy-Tailed to Sub-Gaussian Assumptions
Agentic-Teacher: An Agentic Data Engine for Failure-Driven VLA Post-Training
summary: Improving a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model requires demonstrations that address its weaknesses and provide effective supervision for learning. Coding agents can autonomously generate demonstrations through environment interaction, yet successful execution alone does not ensure effective supervision for VLA learning. We introduce Agentic-Teacher, an autonomous data engine for failure-driven VLA post-training. Given a VLA checkpoint, a task specification, and configured environment tools, the engine analyzes failed rollouts, selects intervention states, and iteratively develops closed-loop code policies through execution feedback. Validated policies become reusable demonstration generators that collect successful continuations from states where the VLA struggles. To make these demonstrations suitable for learning, Agentic-Teacher introduces temporally correlated action noise to broaden state-action coverage, removes idle frames while preserving gripper transitions, and filters trajectories using the frozen base model's flow-matching loss. The resulting demonstrations are combined with successful VLA rollouts for post-training, yielding an updated policy that operates without coding-agent assistance. Agentic-Teacher thus connects the weaknesses of a target VLA to both the generation and curation of its training data. In simulation, it improves $π_0$ success rates from 79.4% to 87.8% on LIBERO-10, from 80.4% to 90.6% on MetaWorld-10, and from 0% to 30.0% across three RoboCasa tasks.

title: X-Strata: Separating Aneurysms and Overlapping Vessels into Layers from 2D X-ray Angiography
comment: 22 pages, including 10 pages of supplementary material
summary: An X-ray angiogram sums every structure along a ray into one pixel. When vessels cross an aneurysm, they obscure part of it and mix their contrast into its filling curve. We present X-Strata, a network that separates a cine angiogram into three layers: the complete aneurysm sac, the vessels in front of it, and the vessels behind it. Contrast timing indicates how much each layer contributes to a pixel, and parallax between two views indicates their order, which a single view cannot determine. X-Strata first estimates the layers and their contrast curves, then uses the second view to assign vessels to the front or back layer, and lifts all layers into 3D. It learns from layer labels projected from same-session 3D rotational angiography, but needs only 2D cine runs and their acquisition geometry at inference. On 220 held-out patients from three centers (122 external), two-view X-Strata ranks first among 14 baselines, including VGGT and C$^2$RV, in recovering the sac where vessels overlap it (Dice 0.693 internal, 0.641 external) and in ordering the layers (balanced accuracy 0.703, 0.659). Its order accuracy exceeds that of all 11 end-to-end baselines by at least 4.1 points internally and 3.3 externally (Holm-adjusted $p < 0.001$) and grows with view separation. Recovered 3D sac surfaces have a median Chamfer distance of 0.34 mm on the internal cohort. X-Strata may therefore provide layered aneurysm and vessel information, including 3D sac shape, for patients who undergo only 2D angiography.

title: Interpretable confidence regions for causal discovery
summary: Most work in causal discovery focuses on point estimation of the underlying causal graph, while uncertainty in the learned structure has received substantially less attention. We develop confidence regions for the completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG) identified from observational data. Our approach builds on perturbed PC (Chang et al., 2026), which generates plausible CPDAGs by perturbing the conditional independence tests underlying the widely used PC algorithm. The threshold used in these tests controls how perturbations translate into variation across the resulting CPDAGs. We propose a new thresholding strategy that suppresses spurious variation across runs while preserving asymptotic coverage, producing a substantially tighter collection of plausible CPDAGs. This collection is summarized through confidence balls and model confidence intervals constructed from the partially ordered set of CPDAGs under model inclusion. We also develop new theory and algorithms for the exact computation of these regions. Simulations show that our confidence regions attain good coverage while being substantially smaller and more interpretable than the original perturbed PC collections.

title: Can LLMs Write Backdoors? An Empirical Security Study of Weight-Space Programming
summary: Recent advances in weight-space programming (WSP) have demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can directly inspect and modify neural network weights without conventional gradient-based training. While this capability opens new possibilities for model improvement, it also raises an important security question: Can LLMs exploit weight-space programming to inject backdoors into neural networks? To answer this question, we present an empirical security study of LLM-driven weight-space programming for backdoor injection. Specifically, we investigate whether general-purpose LLMs can directly modify the weights of target models according to natural-language instructions, without accessing task-specific data, performing forward passes, or computing gradients. We evaluate five LLMs as weight editors across three target architectures: an MLP on MNIST, ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on AG News. Our experiments reveal three key findings. First, LLM-driven weight editing can successfully inject backdoors across different architectures while largely preserving clean performance. Second, successful attacks can require remarkably few parameter modifications, including only six parameters for the MLP and 0.02% of the weights for a fine-tuned Qwen model. Third, editing capabilities vary substantially across LLMs and target architectures: although all five LLMs successfully backdoor the MLP, only GPT-6 Astra succeeds across all three targets. These findings highlight an emerging security risk of weight-space programming and underscore the importance of safeguarding LLM-driven weight editing.

title: Graph Neural Network Prediction of Frequency Nadir and RoCoF Under Topology Variations
summary: Accurate prediction of frequency dynamics under varying network topologies is essential for rapid frequency security assessment, whereas repeated electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations are computationally intensive. This paper develops a topology-aware graph neural network with a radial basis function Kolmogorov-Arnold network (RBF-KAN) regression head, termed RK-GNN, to predict frequency nadir and maximum absolute rate of change of frequency (RoCoF). Scenarios combine load scaling, regional load redistribution, and generator redispatch with intact, N-1, and N-2 transmission topologies. After checks for network connectivity, generator reference limits, and numerical consistency, the retained scenarios are simulated in PSCAD to construct the reference dataset. The RK-GNN is evaluated against a conventional deep neural network (DNN) and a baseline GNN. On the IEEE 39-bus system, the RK-GNN reduces the mean absolute errors (MAEs) of nadir and RoCoF by 48% and 59% relative to the DNN and by 42% and 61% relative to the baseline GNN. Incorporating the bridge indicator and disturbance hop distance yields further MAE reductions of 27% and 54%. These results show that the proposed topology-aware architecture provides accurate prediction of both frequency metrics under varying topologies and substantially reduces the need for repeated EMT simulations.

title: Estimand-specific bootstrap confidence intervals after optimism correction for prediction models
comment: 38 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Supporting Information included after the main article
summary: Confidence intervals after bootstrap optimism correction are often reported for prediction models, but what they cover depends on the estimand. We distinguish two estimands: the target-population performance of the final model developed from the observed sample, $θ_{\mathrm{FM},n}$, and the average performance over repeated model development, $θ_{\mathrm{proc},n}$. Using first-order expansions of the estimation errors, we identify the bootstrap root that matches the error for $θ_{\mathrm{FM},n}$. We use this root in the nested error bootstrap (NEB) as a new reference method, and we show that the optimism error bootstrap (OEB), which needs no inner bootstrap, approximates NEB. We also show that the conventional two-stage bootstrap (TSB) and location-shifted bootstrap (LSB) reproduce the first-order variation for $θ_{\mathrm{proc},n}$. In simulations, NEB generally achieved coverage closer to the nominal level than TSB and LSB for the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, Brier score, and log loss. OEB was close to NEB at moderate to high events per variable (EPV) but could give narrower intervals at low EPV. The distinction is particularly clear for calibration measures: first-order effects of perturbing the training and evaluation distributions cancel in the TSB root, yielding a degenerate first-order limit. In contrast, the NEB root has a nondegenerate first-order limit and yields asymptotically valid confidence intervals for $θ_{\mathrm{FM},n}$ under regularity conditions. Consistent with theory, TSB showed substantial undercoverage for calibration even at larger sample sizes. Our findings emphasize the need to construct confidence intervals for a specified estimand and performance measure.

title: Improved Closed-Form Identification of the Air-Gap Permeance in Magnetic Equivalent Circuits of Rotor-Eccentric Electric Motors
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Fast and accurate simulation of electric motors is essential for their design, fault diagnosis and control. Magnetic equivalent circuits (MECs) offer a computationally efficient alternative to the finite element method (FEM), yet their flux tube representation poorly captures the air-gap field. This creates a challenge, as the air gap stores most of the magnetic energy and governs the electromagnetic torque and, in rotor-eccentric motors, the unbalanced magnetic pull (UMP). Existing air-gap permeance expressions vary widely in their results for torque ripple and UMP and account for tooth-normal eccentricity only. This paper proposes the dual-term air-gap permeance (DTAP) model, a closed-form expression for the air-gap permeance between a stator and a rotor tooth that accounts for tooth-normal and tooth-tangential eccentricity, with and without rotor skew. Its parameters are identified from a FEM model of the air gap and the complete set of tooth heads, which includes the shielding by the neighbouring teeth. For three motors, DTAP reproduces the FEM air-gap permeance with a 2.8-4.8 times smaller error than the state of the art, at a comparable computational cost. Implemented in the MEC of an eccentric induction motor, it reproduces the torque ripple within 1.6% and the peak UMP within 1.3% of the reference, i.e., with 2.8 and 27 times smaller deviations than the state of the art. DTAP thereby enables MEC to predict the torque pulsations and bearing loads of eccentric motors more accurately without sacrificing computational speed.

title: A Consistent Bayesian Adaptive Quotient Graph Framework for Graph-Informed Random Partition Models
summary: Bayesian graph-informed random partition models are widely used to model heterogeneity in structured data. A prominent approach assigns a prior directly on the space of contiguous partitions of a pre-determined graph G; however, such models are not data-adaptive and can be computationally infeasible for large graphs. To address these limitations, we propose a Bayesian adaptive quotient graph framework that induces partitions through a two-level hierarchical prior: a prior is first imposed on quotient graphs of G, followed by a conditional prior on a reduced contiguous partition space induced by each quotient graph. We develop high-level assumptions that guide the construction of the two-level prior such that the reduced space retains desirable partitions. We further establish high-level assumptions for posterior concentration on desirable quotient graphs and partitions. The framework can be readily embedded into many existing Bayesian hierarchical models with latent cluster structures as a contiguous random partition prior. As a specific example, we apply the proposed framework to the spatial random partition model proposed in Huang and Sang (2026). The resulting model adapts to the unknown number of clusters, achieves a faster clustering-consistency contraction rate, and yields substantially lower partition error and computation time in simulations. Finally, we apply the resulting model to a large spatial transcriptomics dataset to demonstrate its practical utility.

title: Alignment with Reflect-Reasoning: Learning How To Follow Principles
summary: The appropriate governing norms and principles for the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) often depend on cultural context and deployment application. However, most alignment techniques focus on training models to conform to human preferences or constitutional principles specified at training time and subsequently fixed. In practice, many deployers rely on system prompting to implement contextual norms and guardrails at inference time. Prior work has shown that post-generation reflective reasoning with critique and revision can improve conformance compared to simple system prompting, but such methods are limited to the reasoning abilities inherent in the trained model. We introduce Reflect-Reasoning, a training method that teaches models how to reason about alignment to principles, rather than simply which principles to follow. Across five models, Reflect-Reasoning consistently outperforms both system prompting and explicit prompting strategies for in-context reflective reasoning. These improvements extend and generalize to entirely out-of-distribution domains of medical and financial principles. We additionally demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning reduces the occurrence of rare but serious principle violations. Finally, we show that Reflect-Reasoning does not erode the safety engineering of a model and is robust against jailbreaking attempts using adversarial constitutions. Overall, our results demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning is a scalable method for training constitutional alignment as a generalizable reasoning capability, enabling models to adapt to novel principles and produce transparent reasoning traces without additional fine-tuning.

title: Implicit discretization of PID-like sliding-mode control with third-order output accuracy
comment: Extended version of a paper submitted to Automatica. 20 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Code and verification records: https://github.com/MartinZapf/Implicit-PID-like
summary: A digital PID-like sliding-mode controller is proposed for a double integrator with a Lipschitz matched disturbance. A proper implicit discretization, matched to the exact sampled dynamics of the plant, attains the accuracy of the continuous-time controller without discretization chattering. Global finite-step convergence to a discrete-time sliding mode is established for two gain designs and every sampling time, using an implicit Lyapunov function and a computer-assisted certificate in exact arithmetic. The resulting controller provides third-order output accuracy, second-order accuracy for its derivative, and exact finite-time rejection of constant matched disturbances. These accuracy orders are proved to be optimal among deterministic causal controllers using the same sampled information.

title: Stratified Randomization Incorporating Historical Control Data
comment: 29 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables, 1 algorithm, Presented at ISCB-GMDS 2026, Freiburg, Germany
summary: Randomized controlled trials are often infeasible in rare diseases because of limited sample size, high costs, or lengthy durations. Hybrid control designs address this by combining a concurrent control arm with historical data. However, existing methods such as propensity score matching (PSM) borrow historical data only at the analysis stage, which limits power gains when covariate distributions differ between historical and concurrent data. We propose a stratified block randomization method for hybrid control trials. Within each stratum, more concurrent subjects are allocated to the treatment arm than to the concurrent control arm, and the difference is filled with historical controls so that the treatment and hybrid control arms are balanced 1:1; once the available historical controls in the stratum are used or a pre-specified overall cap is reached, allocation returns to 1:1. Historical controls are incorporated either by sampling or by weighting. We compared both methods with PSM in terms of type I error rate, power, and sample size via Monte Carlo simulations. The sampling method maintained the type I error rates when there was neither heterogeneity in the outcome model nor unmeasured covariates. It also had power comparable to or greater than that of PSM, particularly when historical controls were unevenly distributed across strata. The power of the weighting method increased with the pooled historical sample size, but its type I error rate was inflated when covariates beyond the stratification factors were present or when stratification factors were dichotomized from continuous covariates. The proposed method incorporates historical data at the allocation stage rather than only at the analysis stage, enabling more efficient use of historical data.

title: ParseBench-2: Severity-Aware Evaluation of Document Parsing
summary: Document-parsing metrics can give high scores to outputs that change important facts and penalize changes that preserve meaning. People can often judge these consequences more easily than they can design a metric to measure them. We introduce a method for developing parsing metrics from severity policies that specify how each error type should affect the score. We express these policies through test scenarios that specify how a metric should behave. We then optimize the metric implementations against these fixed expectations, using coding agents to refine comparison rules, error detectors and weights under human review. This makes stated human priorities an explicit objective of metric design. We apply this method in ParseBench-2, a comprehensive document-parsing benchmark that combines broad capability coverage with metrics calibrated to error severity. It covers 4,317 pages across six dimensions of parsing quality: text, formatting, tables, charts, visual grounding, and forms. We use detailed annotations and targeted difficult cases to check for changed facts, broken structural relationships, and missing content. We take the lower of a parsing score that measures content recovery and a severity cap that penalizes detected errors, so recovering most of a page cannot hide a serious error. Across six severity test suites, our metrics more closely match the expert judgments expressed by the scenario targets than existing metrics and penalize at most 3.4% of the tested benign variations. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation spanning frontier vision-language models, specialized document parsers and open-weight systems, comparing their overall rankings, performance across parsing capabilities and tradeoffs between accuracy and cost.

title: PLL-Less Synchronization of Grid-Following Converters Using a Voltage-Driven Frenet Frame
summary: In grid-following converters, the synchronization path can transmit voltage disturbances to the current loop under weak or unbalanced grid conditions. This paper develops a Frenet-frame controller that derives its axes from the integral curve of the measured voltage at the point of common coupling. The tangential current governs active power, while the normal and binormal currents govern the transverse components of non-active power. Feedforward terms derived from the output filter model compensate curvature and torsion coupling, yielding identical nominal current dynamics across the axes. The controller operates without a phase-locked loop or sequence extraction. A reduced transverse model accounts for the finite bandwidth of geometric rate reconstruction and predicts a reduction in low-frequency coupling from voltage disturbances to current. Controller hardware-in-the-loop tests using real-time simulation of a three-phase four-wire converter show the shortest settling time after an active power reference step and the smallest peak power deviations during balanced voltage disturbances among the tested controllers. Under single-phase voltage unbalance, the method reduces peak binormal current and maximum phase-current total harmonic distortion relative to both benchmarks. It also settles to the commanded power in a weak-grid connection test where the phase-locked loop benchmark exhibits sustained oscillations.

title: High-Dimensional Gaussian and Bootstrap Approximation: Near $1/\sqrt{n}$ Rates with General Covariance
summary: We consider Berry-Esseen bounds over rectangles for sums of $n$ random vectors in $\mathbb{R}^p$ that are i.i.d. A longstanding open question in high-dimensional probability and statistics is whether bounds of order $1/\sqrt n$ are attainable up to factors of $\log(pn)$ when the population covariance matrix is unrestricted. We answer this question affirmatively, provided that the random vectors have sub-Gaussian entries with non-zero variance. In addition, we provide analogous results for bootstrap approximation and Gaussian comparison, which make use of a special discrepancy measure between covariance matrices that enables improvement with respect to prior work. Taking an approach based on interpolation, the novel aspects of the proofs deal with bounding the interpolation derivatives in a way that is not sensitive to the covariance structure.

title: WETW: Learning Pair-Specific Weighted Euclidean Distances for Efficient DTW Search
summary: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is the standard distance for similarity search over time series that are misaligned in time, but its cost is quadratic in the series length and lower bounds often prune few candidates, so search over large collections of long series is slow. Learned approximations embed the series to make comparisons cheap, yet compare every pair with the same fixed rule, usually the Euclidean distance, although DTW aligns each pair differently.
