We observe that, once a pair is aligned, DTW is a Euclidean distance over coordinates selected for that pair. Building on this view, we propose Weighted Euclidean Time Warping (WETW), a learned distance that adapts the comparison of fixed-length embeddings to each pair. A small symmetric network predicts one weight per embedding di- mension and pair without computing an alignment, which halves the error of the best static distance on the same embeddings. The embeddings come from the Weighted Euclidean SEries Encoder (WESEE), whose multi-scale Temporal Feature Extractor keeps the timing information that global pooling removes and raises recall@1 from 0.90 to 0.95, although WETW works with any encoder. We also show that fitting DTW distances is not enough for search, as regression alone misorders the closest neighbours, and that ranking regularization raises recall@1 from 0.79 to 0.95. Our filter-and-verify pipeline, WETW-FV, uses WETW to build a shortlist and exact DTW to check it, so the search is approximate but every returned distance is exact. Over eight datasets, WETW-FV is 11.4x faster than the fastest exact method among the UCR Suite, lower bounds and MESSI-DTW, at a mean recall@10 of 0.93, while the best learned baseline reaches 0.59 at the same speed. On 48K-point series, WETW- FV remains 40x faster than the UCR Suite at a recall@10 of 0.91.

title: Anomalous Sound Detection Using Separation Features and Paired-Mixture Representation Learning
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures; 6-page supplementary material included as an ancillary file. Submitted to IEEE Sensors Journal
summary: Acoustic condition monitoring often relies on normal recordings with limited operating-condition information. This study proposes an anomalous sound detection system that learns from normal recordings without external pre-training and uses machine-type information to organize training and normal references. A separator learns target-component estimation from mixtures of normal target and non-target recordings. With the separator frozen, regional attention and multi-stage fusion are trained on paired mixtures sharing a target, using contrastive and target-reference consistency objectives. Paired-mixture embedding differences provide covariance statistics for correction with normal-reference centering, followed by cosine nearest-neighbor scoring. On Task 2 development-test data from the 2022 Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events challenge, the two-block, 64-channel system achieves an overall harmonic mean of 64.56% on average across three independent training and evaluation runs, with a sample standard deviation of 0.33 percentage points. This mean exceeds that of direct paired-mixture learning by 2.23 percentage points and is 0.31 percentage points below that of the evaluated distillation system using an externally pre-trained teacher. For the learned embeddings, cosine nearest-neighbor scoring outperforms the evaluated Mahalanobis scorers based on global normal statistics. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining separation-based representation learning, interference-based correction, and local normal-reference scoring for anomalous sound detection without detailed operating metadata.

title: Statistical guarantees for signature kernel ridge regression
comment: Keywords: Path space regression, Signature transform, Rough paths, Functional data analysis, Kernel methods
summary: Path signatures are a standard tool for learning functionals on path space. The main underpinnings of their application are universal approximation results. For a wide range of function classes on path space, these results state that any function in such a class can be approximated arbitrarily well by a linear functional of the path signature. Hence, linear functionals of the signature are in principle expressive enough for learning functions on path space. Nonetheless, these results do not provide insights into the statistical question of how much data is needed to identify a suitable signature functional. In this work, we study this question in the framework of kernel ridge regression with the signature kernel. The target is the conditional expectation $\E[Y|X]$, where $X$ is the observed path and $Y$ is a real-valued response. Under different assumptions on the moments of the signature kernel and the response, we provide finite-sample and consistency guarantees for the method. We supplement our theoretical analysis with numerical experiments that illustrate our results.

title: Real-Time Diffusion Relighting as a Neural Sensor: Closing the Low-Light Domain Gap for Robotic Perception
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026. Project page: https://shengjie-xu.com/conferences/2026_IROS_neural-sensor/
summary: Low-light conditions severely degrade robotic perception: object detectors trained on daylight imagery are prone to failure under dark and adverse weather conditions that fall outside of their training distribution. Furthermore, from an efficiency standpoint, existing Low-Light Image Enhancement (LLIE) methods are designed for offline processing and are therefore impractical to integrate into live control loops. To address these issues, we propose to embed a Generative Neural Sensor within the control loop that treats illumination as a generative prior rather than a signal processing problem, enabling task-relevant semantic recovery. We further propose an Real-Time Perceptual Architecture that decouples high-latency semantic recovery from low-latency robotic control. Rather than blocking the control loop, our system runs a large-scale image-to-image diffusion model in a background thread, and is activated only when a drop in detection confidence signals a perceptual uncertainty event, significantly reducing computational overhead. Our method sets a new state-of-the-art performance on the ExDark low-light benchmark with 87.1% mAP, and under adverse weather conditions, significantly boosts detection rates over competing methods. On a navigation task in a closed-loop autonomous driving simulator (CARLA), we achieve a 100% lap completion rate, establishing a simulation-based proof-of-concept for integrating high-latency generative models with standard robotic control autonomy stacks.

title: Few-Shot Open-Set Hyperspectral Pixel-Wise Classification with Spatial Aware Label Propagation
summary: Pixelwise classification of hyperspectral images (HSI) is a fundamental task in remote sensing, but its deployment in real-world applications is often limited by the scarcity of labeled data and the presence of unknown classes at inference time. In this work, we propose Few-shot Open-set hyperspectral recognition from Self-Supervised Learning training (FOSSeL), a unified framework for few-shot, open-set hyperspectral pixelwise classification that does not require supervised training. The proposed approach first leverages self-supervised learning to construct a discriminative feature space from unlabeled data. Then, given a small set of labeled seed pixels, class predictions are obtained through spatially-aware graph-based label propagation over superpixel representations, enabling the joint exploitation of spectral similarity and spatial consistency. To address the open-set scenario, we introduce simple yet effective strategies to identify pixels that do not belong to the known classes. We evaluate FOSSeL on three benchmark hyperspectral datasets under multiple few-shot settings. The results show that the proposed framework achieves competitive or superior performance compared to fully supervised methods while maintaining robustness in the presence of unknown classes. These findings highlight the potential of combining self-supervised feature learning with graph-based inference for practical HSI analysis in low-annotation and open-world scenarios.

title: Efficient and Practical Clustering of Variables in Causal Graphs
summary: Clustering variables in a graph may improve visual clarity and simplify causal inference. Harnessing the full potential of clustering requires an automated method to detect useful clusters in a graph. We introduce a novel class of clusters called conduits, and present a sound, complete and efficient algorithm for detecting all conduits in the graph. In addition to algorithmic detectability, conduits appear naturally in causal graphs stemming from real-world applications, enabling substantial size reduction. Furthermore, the structure of conduits enables the application of known identifiability results regarding clustering. We demonstrate these properties in a simulation study with real-world graphs.

title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories
comment: Accepted at the 1st Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB) at NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com/SWE-rebench/trajectory-analyzer
summary: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, and audit its predictions against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. We find that agents with similar solve rates can nevertheless differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify code. Moreover, without using task outcomes, token counts, or tool names as features, aggregate behavioral profiles retrieve the corresponding agent stack across disjoint repository sets and programming languages, although task composition is not fully controlled in the cross-repository setting. Through analyses of frontier models and agent scaffolds, we further show that scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift agents' search, editing, and testing behavior. We release the deterministic parser together with the full annotation and analysis pipeline alongside an annotated trajectory subset.

title: Enhancing Transient Stability of VSG-Controlled Converters Under Grid Frequency Disturbances
summary: Strong damping feedback can substantially improve the transient synchronization stability of renewable energy converters employing virtual synchronous generator (VSG) control. However, conventional damping feedback uses the nominal frequency as its reference. When the frequency of a weak grid deviates from nominal, strong damping tends to keep the VSG frequency near nominal. This can sustain a frequency difference between the VSG and the grid and compromise transient synchronization. To address this problem, this paper proposes a complex-frequency-based method to estimate the grid reference frequency from local terminal measurements. The estimated frequency replaces the nominal reference in the VSG synchronization loop, so that damping acts on the frequency difference between the VSG and the real grid. Controller hardware-in-the-loop tests validate the effectiveness of the proposed method under grid frequency disturbances and its robustness to grid parameter uncertainty and adverse grid conditions.

title: evgmrf: An R Package For Gaussian Markov Random Field Extreme Value Models
summary: We introduce \textsf{evgmrf}, an \textsf{R} package for fitting spatially varying extreme value models using Gaussian Markov random fields (GMRFs). The package supports the generalized extreme value distribution for block maxima, the generalized Pareto distribution for threshold exceedances, the Poisson--GPD point-process model, and the $r$-largest order-statistics model. Distributional parameters may vary over regular spatial grids or arbitrary regions that can be represented by a valid adjacency matrix, with optional fixed effects and covariate dependence. Spatial structure is represented through intrinsic conditional autoregressive, proper conditional autoregressive, and Besag--York--Mollié 2 models, which are extended with non-Gaussian random-effect distributions. Estimation uses penalized likelihood with smoothing or dependence hyper-parameters estimated using a Laplace approximation, exploiting sparse precision matrices for computational efficiency. The package provides methods for model summaries, spatial visualization, prediction on link and response scales, estimation of extreme quantiles, and uncertainty quantification in the form of approximate standard error estimates, or via simulations from parameter sampling distributions. Examples based on gridded and county-level precipitation data illustrate the use of the package for spatial modelling of environmental extremes. \textsf{evgmrf} provides a unified, accessible framework for extreme value analyses in which distributional parameters exhibit structured spatial variation.

title: Racing the Clock: Teaching VLNs Budget-Conditioned Object Search
summary: A rescue robot entering a building with thirty seconds on the clock should sprint toward the single most promising room; given ten minutes, it should instead explore a broader tour. Yet vision-language-navigation (VLN) models are typically evaluated under a fixed episode limit that the policy never observes, even though time-critical missions require behavior to adapt to the available budget. We study budget-conditioned object search: given a target category and an explicit action budget, an agent must find as many distinct target instances as possible before the budget expires. We investigate how to supervise VLNs for this task by comparing a privileged TSP expert, which plans near-optimal routes using the full map and true target locations, with a room-level Bellman expert that maximizes expected return under partial observability using high-level cross-scene semantic priors. Despite the TSP expert achieving substantially higher expert performance, its demonstrations are less effective for learning exploration: on held-out HM3D scenes, the Bellman-supervised VLN consistently outperforms the TSP-supervised VLN, with the advantage becoming more pronounced at longer budgets. At 2000 steps (500m), the Bellman-supervised VLN finds 71.4% of reachable target instances, compared with 65.5% for the TSP-supervised VLN and 44.8% for the pretrained VLN. These results highlight a distinction between optimal routing and optimal exploration: effective exploration supervision should optimize decisions under partial observability rather than imitate routes that are optimal only once the environment is fully known.

title: BeST: Beta splatted tomography for direct reconstruction from coherent imaging measurements
summary: Conventional coherent X-ray tomography requires the phase of each projection to be reconstructed with high fidelity. However, individual reconstructed projections might be flawed, e.g. due to positioning errors, yielding inconsistent tomographic reconstructions. By directly coupling phase retrieval and tomography, consistency is enforced through a common object volume. But reconstructing a full volume demands substantial computational resources. To reduce this demand, we introduce Beta Splatted Tomography (BeST), which represents the common object volume using compactly supported beta primitives with closed-form analytical projections, enabling efficient reconstruction directly from coherent scattering images. This representation substantially reduces the number of optimizable parameters compared to a voxel grid. We demonstrate BeST on experimental datasets from hard X-ray near-field holography and far-field ptychography measurements. In both cases, the joint technique improves reconstruction quality compared to two-step methods.

title: Does Increasing Government Spending on Tertiary Education Provide a Return on Investment? A Bayesian Causal Inference Analysis
comment: 37 pages, 10 figures, 10 tables. Open-source R/C++ code, data, and interactive policy web application available at https://github.com/andrewcparnell/education-tax-bcf
summary: When a government increases public spending on tertiary (university) education, does it provide a positive fiscal return on investment once general economic growth is separated out? Cross-country data make this hard to answer because growing economies naturally collect more tax, international ratios divide per-student spending by GDP per person and student headcount, and cohorts take years to graduate. We assemble a five-year panel of 121 countries (1985-2024) and fit continuous-treatment Multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests that model four tax changes jointly whilst adjusting for starting conditions, predicted funding, and follow-up economic growth. A +10 percentage-point (pp) increase in per-student university spending (% of GDP per person) shifts the tax mix toward direct income and profit taxation by +0.36 pp after 5 years (93% probability of a positive effect) and +0.71 pp after 10 years (96% probability). Overall tax-to-GDP takes a decade to respond as cohorts graduate: 10-year total non-resource tax rises by +0.24 pp of GDP (89% probability) and direct income tax by +0.12 pp (90% probability) per +10 pp of per-student spending, by +0.37 pp (100% probability) after five-year within-country funding increases, and by +0.22 pp in total tax (95% probability) and +0.15 pp in direct income tax (98% probability) per +25% increase in real PPP dollars per student. Comparing one entering cohort's degree cost against its 40-year career tax payments shows a typical three- to five-fold total tax return in high-income economies (EUR 2.37 billion in Ireland returning EUR 9.66 billion in total tax with a 77% probability of net profit and EUR 2.87 billion in direct income tax, or EUR 11.55 billion in the UK returning EUR 58.33 billion), whereas expanding the university budget without protecting spending per student yields no return.

title: A Cut Finite Element Method with Boundary Value Correction for Robin, Neumann and Interface Conditions
summary:
We extend the cut finite element method with boundary value correction of Burman, Hansbo and Larson [Math.\ Comp.\ 87 (2018) 633--657] to Robin and Neumann conditions and to interface problems with imperfect bonding. The formulation retains a piecewise affine boundary for all integration, while using the exact geometry only at boundary quadrature points.
  The correction uses Taylor expansions of the solution and its gradient along the discrete normal, with the exact normal used to evaluate the transported flux. At an interface, a further correction to the normal flux jump accounts for the difference between these two normals. Under the stated trace and Poincaré bounds, the corrected form is an $O(h^{1/2})$ perturbation of a symmetric form, whose matrix can therefore be used as a preconditioner.
  For a fixed finite Robin coefficient, we obtain the energy error bound $C_β(h^p+δ_h^{m+1})$, whereas the bound uniform in the Robin coefficient is $C(h^p+h^{-1/2}δ_h^{m+1})$, provided the Poincaré constant is uniform. With $δ_h=O(h^2)$, the sufficient Taylor orders are therefore $2m+2\ge p$ and $2m+\frac32\ge p$, respectively. Numerical examples for $p=1,2,3$ illustrate these rates and the effect of the flux-jump correction in the interface problem.

title: Constant-Weight Sparse Vector Coded Augmented-AFDM
summary: Sparse vector coding (SVC) and its variants convey information through sparse vectors (SVs), or sparse support patterns and detecting information by solving sparse recovery problems, making them attractive for short-packet ultra-reliable low-latency communications (URLLC). However, as the required information rate increases, conventional SVC schemes or the enhanced SVC (ESVC) schemes require a rapidly growing number of SVs, resulting in significant increase of complexity and receiver processing latency. On the other hand, when communicating in doubly selective channels, orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) suffers from the Doppler spread induced inter-carrier interference, while affine frequency division multiplexing (AFDM) experiences the same peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) problem as OFDM, although it allows diversity gain from channel's double selectivity. To address these issues, this paper proposes a constant-weight sparse vector coded augmented AFDM (CW-SVC/A$^2$FDM ) scheme, along with a corresponding joint support and symbol detection algorithm. In this scheme, SVs are represented by constant-weight codewords that feature a fixed Hamming weight and a large Hamming distance, resulting in relatively small SV sets. Simulation results compare various SVC/ESVC schemes and diverse coding schemes employed by the CW-SVC/A$^2$FDM, including Hamming, BCH, RS, and polar codes, for QAM symbol protection. The results demonstrate that the proposed scheme provides a distinct reliability advantage over conventional SVC/ESVC schemes, achieving a gain of up to 14 dB. Furthermore, the study indicates that the CWC's weight and minimum Hamming distance must be carefully selected to balance detection reliability, QAM modulation order, and sparse recovery feasibility, thereby maximizing the overall system's performance.

title: Training-point consistency of kernel ridge regression with varying correlation scales
summary: The scale parameter in kernel ridge regression plays a pivotal role in modeling the correlation structure of data. In modern applications, sampling density and the underlying correlation range often change simultaneously, making a fixed-scale assumption highly restrictive. However, establishing asymptotic theories under varying scale parameters is fundamentally challenging. To address this gap, this paper develops a unified theoretical framework for kernel ridge regression under varying scale parameters. We establish that, on uniform tensor grids with product exponential kernels, the consistency of the training-point risk holds if and only if the effective local sample size diverges to infinity. This sharp criterion universally covers all regimes along arbitrary deterministic scale sequences, seamlessly unifying the long-range, fixed-scale, and short-range. Furthermore, we provide an explicit, signal-independent construction of a deterministic regularization penalty that guarantees this consistency. Numerical experiments illustrate the criterion and the corresponding penalty across all the three regimes.

title: TSGP-2: On the Non-Linearity of Symbolic Regression Problems and How to Exploit It with Model-based Semantic Genetic Programming
summary: Model-based variation operators such as the one used in Transformer Semantic Genetic Programming (TSGP) are affected by possible biases of their training data. TSGP is trained, in particular, on programs generated by Genetic Programming (GP) runs on linear target functions, which leads to a bias toward linear offspring. This bias can hinder search performance on problems that require non-linear solutions. This work has two goals: first, it investigates the linearity of standard test problems such as the Feynman and real-world benchmark problems. While most of the structure of real-world problems can be well approximated by linear structures, the Feynman problems exhibit varying levels of non-linear structure. Thus, a proper variation operator of a search method should be able to create both types of programs, linear as well as non-linear ones. Motivated by this observation, we propose TSGP-2, which follows the functionality of TSGP but uses as training data programs from GP runs on both linear and non-linear target functions. As a result, the training data includes a lower share of programs that behave linearly (the share drops from 83% to 37%). With a higher share of non-linear structures, TSGP-2 outperforms TSGP on problems with non-linear structure, while performing similarly on linear problems. In addition, TSGP-2 is less biased toward linear offspring and is able to propose a higher number of meaningful non-linear offspring earlier during search, which coincides with better solutions. The findings underscore the importance of training data for a learned variation operator and emphasize that the biases of search operators should be aligned with the problems they are applied to.

title: Data-Driven Output Regulation via Predictive Control
summary: This paper addresses constrained output regulation for unknown linear systems by means of predictive control directly from input-output data. The objective is to reject disturbances and track references generated by a known exosystem, without identifying a plant model or solving the output regulator equations. The first step is a trajectory parametrization for plants driven by exosignals with known dynamics. % By exploiting the known exosystem eigenstructure, Willems et al's fundamental lemma is extended from autonomous input-output trajectories to trajectories coupled with exogenous modes. By exploiting the known exosystem eigenstructure, input-output trajectories driven by an exosignal of known phase are parametrized directly from data, which contains the affine version of Willems et al.'s fundamental lemma as a special case. This parametrization yields a nominal data-driven predictive control (DDPC) regulator, for which a Lyapunov argument proves exponential convergence to the regulator manifold. For periodic exosignals, the steady-state feedforward input is eliminated from the online problem through an incremental-input regularization, leading to an implementable regulator based on measured data and known exosystem information. Bounded output noise is handled by slack and coefficient regularization, with a regularization center computed offline from data; the resulting robust DDPC law is recursively feasible and practically stabilizing, with an ultimate regulation error that vanishes with the noise bound. A constrained lateral vehicle-control example with periodic road curvature illustrates disturbance rejection, input-constraint satisfaction, and the transition from exact regulation with noise-free data to practical regulation with noisy data.

title: Cross-Fitted Doubly Robust Estimation with Student-t Outcome Engines: ECM Algorithms, Monte Carlo Evidence and Schistosomiasis Programme Data from the Democratic Republic of the Congo
comment: 37 pages, 27 figures, 11 tables. Python code (single file) reproducing all analyses and figures provided as an ancillary file
summary: Routine data on preventive chemotherapy for schistosomiasis are confounded, clustered, heavy-tailed and heaped. We study how cross-fitted augmented inverse probability weighted (AIPW) estimators behave, and how they should be computed, when least squares is replaced by Student-t outcome engines: Huber and t iteratively reweighted least squares, and a two-component t scale-mixture regression fitted by an ECM algorithm, alongside a residual-clipped augmentation. We give four short propositions (exact AIPW bias, the efficiency bound, the estimand of clipping, monotone ascent of a scale-constrained ECM), a single-file Python implementation with cluster-level cross-fitting, cluster-robust standard errors and a cluster bootstrap, and a Monte Carlo study with up to 1000 replications per cell. Robust outcome engines leave AIPW unchanged (RMSE differences at most 0.002), whereas clipping cuts RMSE by 26-45% under symmetric contamination, under-covers, and, as a plasmode experiment built on real covariates and residuals shows, shifts the estimand when residual laws differ between arms. One-sided artefacts that differ between arms bias every estimator. Heaped data also break naive code: the MAD scale collapses and the mixture likelihood is unbounded, and we give simple guards. Applied to 1485 rounds in 362 health zones of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (ESPEN, 2014-2025), integrated delivery appears to raise programme coverage by 17.4 percentage points, yet epidemiological coverage differs by only 0.9: the gap comes from targeting denominators, a real differential artefact that no outcome engine can remove.

title: FOMOS: Feature-Oriented Meshing of SDFs
summary: We introduce FOMOS, a purely geometric method for feature-oriented meshing of signed distance functions (SDFs) that addresses various challenges of the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our algorithm improves mesh quality and runtime, enabling the SDF meshing in a matter of seconds. While existing techniques such as Marching Cubes and Neural Dual Contouring either produce dense, low-quality triangulations or sacrifice details for sparsity, often requiring carefully chosen user parameters, our single-parameter FOMOS leverages feature sized sampling to dynamically adjust mesh resolution based on local feature size (LFS), which we compute efficiently by sampling a medial scaffold. The LFS considers not only curvature but also shape thickness and captures large features through non-local structure, omitting many redundant small triangles from existing methods. Through extensive comparisons, we demonstrate the distinct strengths of FOMOS in execution time, reconstructed result accuracy, and triangle quality in the output mesh. We also introduce a lightweight variant of FOMOS targeting huge ($10k^3$) sparse inputs, which, to the best of our knowledge, no existing method can handle except Marching Cubes. To demonstrate the usefulness of our method, we show that FOMOS enables instant previews using a sub-sampled medial scaffold and can accelerate volumetric simulations by orders of magnitude.

title: Latent resonances in oscillator networks
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, Supplementary Materials included (6 figures, 7 tables)
summary: In networks of coupled oscillators, from neural circuits to power grids, damping is expected to suppress oscillations because of its dissipativity. Here we show that local damping can, counterintuitively, amplify oscillations along some input-output channels, while the network's global oscillation energy decreases and its spectral properties improve. The amplified oscillation arises from a latent resonance that lies in the spectrum yet barely manifests. The added passive damping reshapes this resonance by mixing it with adjacent eigenmodes. In random power-grid networks, damping can boost weakly responding channels by more than an order of magnitude, while subdominant channels can grow to exceed the originally strongest channel. Damping thus not only suppresses oscillations but also provides a way to redistribute oscillatory energy. For any passive network, the amplified response and its upper bound follow exactly from baseline quantities, offering a principled route for network design and control.

title: Characterizing M-estimators using canonical divergences from information geometry
summary: On Euclidean space, the losses that produce consistent M-estimators of a functional are its strictly consistent scoring functions (Dimitriadis, Fissler and Ziegel, 2024), and Osband's principle characterizes these through identification functions, which define method-of-moments estimators. We extend this characterization to the probability simplex. We define the residual, which on Euclidean space is a subtraction, as the inverse exponential map of an affine connection. It identifies the exponential barycenter of the connection: the arithmetic, normalized geometric and Fréchet means for the mixture, exponential and Levi-Civita connections. Its integral along geodesics is the canonical divergence of Ay and Amari (2015). A geometric form of Osband's principle decides which losses each connection admits. For the flat connections every strictly convex generator yields a consistent Bregman loss. For the curved $α$-connections, half the squared Fisher-Rao distance is (up to scale) the only consistent loss for the Fréchet mean, and for $α\notin \{-1, 0, 1\}$ no such loss exists and only the method of moments remains. The residual is integrable only at $α= 0$, sharpening the integrability claim of Ay and Amari. The characterization yields the estimating equations of regression on the simplex and the calibration decomposition of compositional forecasts.

title: Classification with Large-Step Gradient Descent: Unifying Self-Stabilization and Convergence Rates
summary: Neural networks are often trained with gradient descent (GD) using step sizes that exceed classical stability thresholds, a regime where standard convergence theory no longer applies. Despite exhibiting non-monotonic loss and oscillatory dynamics, this regime frequently leads to faster convergence and better generalization. Existing theoretical perspectives offer complementary but incomplete insights: one identifies a self-stabilization mechanism that drives GD toward flat regions but does not yield convergence rates; another derives rigorous rates for specific losses but does not explain the underlying stabilization mechanism; and a third unifies these views for overparameterized least squares, but relies on the existence of a minimizer manifold, which is absent in classification settings. In this work, we extend this unified geometric perspective to exponential-tail losses, including logistic and cross-entropy losses in separable linear classification, where the loss infimum is not attained at any finite parameter. We identify a curvature-defined reference subspace that replaces the role of the minimizer manifold, yielding a coupled dynamical system in which orthogonal oscillations are damped by parallel progress along directions of decreasing sharpness. Under regularity conditions, which we verify for logistic and multiclass cross-entropy losses on symmetric data models, we derive explicit bounds for the iterates, not just the loss, covering both the unstable and stable regimes, and revealing a three-phase damping structure in the latter. Our analysis further uncovers a transient implicit bias induced by large step sizes: although GD converges asymptotically to the max-margin direction, large steps can leave persistent orthogonal residuals and, in certain geometries, amplify them, affecting finite-time alignment with the max-margin direction.

title: Recursive Semi-Blind Receivers for Wideband Array Processing
summary: Using the commonly employed uniform rectangular array (URA) as an illustrative example, we have recently shown that the block-term tensor decomposition (BTD) model provides a natural representation for the output signal of a multi-dimensional separable sensor array structure in the presence of channel multipath. A palette of effective and efficient semi-blind joint channel estimation/data detection (JCD) algorithms for URA processing, which wed BTD modeling with existing JCD schemes, has thus been developed, and recently extended so as to be applicable in large-scale arrays and/or time-varying environments. However, both the model and the algorithms were based on the assumption of narrowband signals, arriving through paths of effectively the same delay. In this paper, recursive JCD algorithms for wideband sources are developed and evaluated through simulations in a time-varying setting and across different constellation sizes, in comparison with their batch counterparts and the training-only-based solution. They are seen to enjoy the ability to track channel variations and detect the transmitted symbols `on the fly', with the aid of only a short initial training stage.

title: Detection and Classification in Latent Spaces: High-Dimensional Analysis and Validation
summary: Foundation models produce high-dimensional latent representations in which suitably designed statistical decision rules can be effective yet analytically tractable. We study such detectors in the high-dimensional regime, where latent dimension and training sample size grow proportionally. For linear and quadratic statistics, we derive explicit large-deviation characterizations of false-alarm and miss-detection performance under the Neyman-Pearson paradigm, and show how the binary analysis extends to multi-class classification. The resulting error probabilities and corresponding decay rates exhibit non-monotonic dependence on the shape parameter, including double-descent and, in some regimes, multiple-descent. Experiments on vision, text, and audio datasets using modern foundation models show close agreement between theoretical predictions and empirical performance. In particular, the proposed framework allows us to set a prescribed false-alarm level and accurately predict the corresponding miss-detection probability. Overall, our results provide a theoretically grounded and interpretable framework with competitive empirical performance across different modalities.

title: Unfinished-Bench: Measuring Rule Violations by Persistent Agents in Realistic Work Environments
summary: AI agents are increasingly equipped with persistence toward task completion to run delegated work autonomously for long periods, under many unstated constraints from internal documents and other people's authority. When completion requires violating a rule, the agent must decide alone, yet benchmarks of instruction-rule conflicts state the rule in the prompt or keep it hidden and do not evaluate persistence. We present Unfinished-Bench, a benchmark that gives models persistence in autonomous runs without a user, in realistic work environments with embedded rules. In each of its 97 scenarios across 7 organizations and 7 risk categories, the goal and the rule cannot both hold. We find that persistence raised violations of a rule in an internal document from 32.2% to 43.6%, five times the 8.5% for the same rule stated by the user. Of the document-rule violations, 98.3% occurred after the rule was displayed, and in 89% of a judged sample the agent first wrote down the rule. Violations of rules placed in the environment without user oversight can lead to serious incidents, so persistence-driven risks need to be evaluated. Benchmark documentation: https://francis21c.github.io/unfinished-bench/

title: Grid-Compliance Testing of Wind Turbines through Virtualized Component Tests: Testing Concept and Test Bench
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables, peer-reviewed journal article
summary: As the proportion of inverter-connected wind turbines increases, test methods for evaluating their grid behavior are becoming increasingly important. This paper presents a Power Hardware-in-the-Loop (PHiL)-based method for grid connection testing of wind turbines. For the first time, geographically distributed simulations of aerodynamics via the Internet and of the grid model via a fiber-optic connection are integrated into certification-relevant tests. The concept expands upon the methods described in IEC TS 61400-21-4. Initial experimental results confirm high emulation quality and sufficiently low latencies, and meet the requirements for a standards-compliant grid emulation.

title: LaMe: a Joint Latent Mediation Framework for High-Dimensional Systems
summary: Mediation analysis seeks to understand how an exposure influences an outcome through intermediate variables. However, as increasingly rich datasets become available, hundreds to thousands of potential mediators make these systems difficult to model and hard to interpret. Latent-variable approaches offer a natural way to accommodate these high-dimensional settings. However, existing latent mediation methods face limitations, including overparameterization, biased inference, or limited scalability. We develop LaMe, a joint linear-Gaussian framework that summarizes a high-dimensional exposure-mediator-outcome system through a small number of latent variables. We identify natural direct and indirect effects under an explicit assumption that the manifest measurements fully capture the latent mediators, and characterize conditions under which the latent representation effectively restricts the observed cross-covariance structure. Simulations assess recovery of observed association parameters, natural effects, and manifest features associated with latent mediation pathways across a range of challenging settings. Four real-world applications demonstrate competitive predictive performance with compact latent representations, including single-dimensional representations of biomarker and proteomic measurements. Together, these results establish LaMe as a practical framework for estimating and summarizing multivariate mediation systems under explicit structural and measurement assumptions.

title: Tracing Knowledge and Reasoning in LLM
comment: This paper was accepted with an A-decision to Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics. This version is the pre-publication version prior to MIT Press production
summary: Current evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) report performance at the dataset or task level, revealing what a model achieves but offering little insight into the internal processing associated with its performance. We propose a task-centric framework for characterising the model-internal processing elicited by a benchmark. It combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to characterise benchmarks spanning a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to surface failure modes that task-level scores conceal. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks and conduct targeted internal-state analyses on representative models and tasks, observing systematic differences in processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks. We shift evaluation from asking what score a model achieves toward characterising the processing patterns associated with that score, potentially supporting more targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice. We open source our code at https://github.com/extraordinarylab/trace-kr.

title: Distributed Output-Feedback Control for Linear Multichannel Systems
summary: This paper investigates distributed output-feedback stabilization of linear multichannel systems in which agents exchange state estimates without disclosing local control inputs or feedback gains. Remote control actions are treated as unknown inputs and geometrically decoupled from stable quotient-error dynamics. The proposed framework accommodates nontrivial intersections of local loss subspaces by retaining the coupling between the plant and common estimation errors. A Hurwitz condition on the coupled dynamics, together with a sufficient consensus-gain bound, guarantees exponential closed-loop convergence for every fixed feedback selection in a compact family. For polytopic feedback families, a quotient-preserving parameterization of output injections enables joint synthesis of nominal feedback and observer gains via alternating linear matrix inequalities, followed by a convex semidefinite program certifying a common consensus gain. A numerical example demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed design.

title: A Bayesian approach to technological emergence, climate variability, and demographic stability in northern South America
comment: 30 pages, 6 Figures, submitted to Journal of Archaeological Science
summary: Human communities produce technology in almost every environment, but the conditions that enable technologies in the tropics are not well understood. We test two competing hypotheses---that technological emergence is triggered by environmental stress and that technology tracks growth in effective populations---by integrating Holocene archaeological and paleoclimate evidence. We use archaeological derived radiocarbon dates from Colombia as a proxy for human activity, including dating plant management, pottery, metallurgy, and raised fields. For palaeoclimate, we use two El Niño--Southern Oscillation (ENSO) reconstructions: Laguna Pallcacocha and Laguna El Junco in Ecuador. A Bayesian changepoint at 3575 cal BP (95% highest posterior density interval (HPDI) = 3811--3329) marks a ~13-fold increase in the growth rate of pre-Hispanic human activity ($r_2$/$r_1$ median = 13.3, 95% HPDI = 8.1--22.2). Plant management and pottery predate this shift by more than a millennium, whereas metallurgy and raised fields cluster within the early acceleration phase, during relative climatic and demographic stability. A Bayesian log-linear regression of human activity on ENSO frequency and intensity after the demographic changepoint reveals an asymmetric covariation: reduced ENSO frequency and intensity suppress activity by 58% and 21%, whereas ENSO frequency raises activity modestly (~11--13%). Therefore, ENSO regulates demographic activity rather than triggering technological emergence. These patterns suggest that pre-Columbian communities may have innovated when they could compute---when an effective population sat above a critical threshold and stability windows permitted combinatorial search---rather than when they were forced to by environmental stress, expressed as demographic or climatic variability.

title: Diffusion Tree Sampling for Inference Time Adaptation of Crystal Generative Models
summary: Diffusion-based generative models have become strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but turning that prior into promising candidates requires steering toward several conflicting properties at once. Fine-tuning is expensive and produces a new model for every new objective, while differentiable guidance is not applicable to many real-world tasks. We instead adapt these generative models at inference time using Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), a Monte Carlo tree search procedure over the denoising trajectory. We make two technical contributions on top of DTS that are particularly relevant for AI-for-science applications. First, we show how to use existing property-conditional generative models (e.g., models fine-tuned for classifier-free guidance) as guided proposals inside DTS, without distorting the target distribution. Second, we extend DTS to multi-objective sampling, so that a single search produces samples spanning an entire Pareto front. We instantiate both adaptations on de novo crystal generation: improving the stability of crystals generated by different models, using pretrained conditional models to generate crystals belonging to rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and generating crystals along a Pareto front of high dielectric constant and high bandgap materials. Across these tasks, DTS-based inference-time adaptation successfully improves model outputs without modifying the models themselves.

title: Beyond Scalar Inertia: Frequency-Response-Based Assessment of Finite-Duration Inertial Support in Grid-Forming Converters
comment: This paper has 6 pages with 5 figures. The target journal will be determined at a later stage
summary: Conventional scalar inertia characterizes only the low-frequency terminal behavior of grid-forming converters (GFMs) and cannot fully predict inertial energy delivery during short-duration frequency disturbances. This letter proposes a frequency-response-based method to assess finite-duration inertial support using complex terminal power--frequency responses, such as those provided by Network Frequency Perturbation (NFP) plots. For GFMs with nonzero steady-state droop, a duration-dependent energy-equivalent inertia is defined after subtracting the ideal static-droop contribution. An exact spectral relationship is established, expressing this metric as a duration-weighted integral of frequency-dependent inertia, without requiring knowledge of the internal controller structure and parameters. The duration dependence of the metric is further shown to encode observable oscillation frequencies and damping ratios. A coefficient-decoupling GFM control with identical scalar inertia and droop across different settings is used for verification.

title: Causal and conditional tail coefficients: asymptotics, inference and graph recovery
summary: The causal tail coefficient (CTC) measures the influence of an extreme value of one variable on another variable and has been proposed as a tool for causal discovery in heavy-tailed models. Despite its popularity, the asymptotic behavior of its empirical counterpart has not been well understood. We develop an asymptotic theory for the rank-based CTC estimator with an intermediate threshold under nonparametric conditions that are satisfied by all standard copula models. A key observation is that the CTC is determined by the mean of a conditional tail limit distribution, which clarifies its interpretation and determines the asymptotic variance of the estimator. We establish joint asymptotic normality for the entire CTC matrix and prove consistency of a multiplier bootstrap for simultaneous inference. For heavy-tailed linear and recursive max-linear structural equation models, we show that the CTC equals one if and only if the first variable is an ancestor of the second, which leads to confidence graphs for the ancestral graph with asymptotic coverage guarantees. All results extend to general conditional tail coefficients, defined as further functionals of the conditional tail limit distribution. A simulation study and an application to dietary intake data illustrate the methods.

title: Availability-Aware Historical Feedback Learning for Electric Arc Furnace Temperature and Chemical Composition Prediction
summary: Electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking plays an increasingly important role in recycled and lower-carbon steel production. However, variability in charged materials, energy input, and operating conditions makes accurate prediction of molten steel temperature and final chemical composition challenging. Intermittent or delayed measurements limit the information available for timely prediction. This study develops an availability-aware historical-feedback learning framework for predicting EAF endpoint temperature and the final concentrations of twelve chemical elements. Eight industrial data sources are integrated into three progressively enriched predictor representations comprising 19 static, 39 temporal, and 47 history-informed features. Historical outcomes are incorporated only when eligible under an assumed 60-minute measurement-release delay. Using 19,738 temperature heats and 3,341 chemistry heats, twelve tuned regression algorithms are evaluated through chronological forward validation. The proposed historical-feedback representation reduces root mean squared error (RMSE) in 147 of 156 matched algorithm-target comparisons. For temperature prediction, ExtraTrees achieves an RMSE of 12.290 degrees C, representing a 5.54 percent reduction compared with its temporal-only counterpart. Historical-feature ablation and feedback-delay sensitivity analyses demonstrate the importance of recent outcome information and its availability. In a separate retrospective later-period evaluation, lightweight adaptive residual correction reduces temperature RMSE from 12.502 to 12.275 degrees C without retraining the underlying model. Exploratory deep learning comparisons and target-specific feature-attribution analyses provide additional insights into predictive behavior. The results establish historical outcome availability and sequential feedback as important considerations for EAF endpoint prediction.

title: Controllability-Informed Distributed Electric Propulsion Aircraft Design Using Probabilistic Attainable Moment Sets
summary: Integrated aircraft design combines models of aerodynamics, propulsion, mass, and mission performance in one design loop, so that the disciplines can be traded against each other from the earliest stage. For configurations with distributed electric propulsion (DEP), part of the control authority comes from the propulsion system itself, which directly affects the required size of the tail and should therefore be known while the aircraft is being sized. This paper presents a controllability measure that is evaluated for every design in the loop and returned to it as a design signal. The attainable moment set of each candidate design is computed from the surrugate models of the loop and it is compared with a required moment set. Since the low-fidelity surrugate models are uncertain, the comparison is formulated with probabilistic attainable moment sets: the uncertainty is propagated to the boundary of the set, which yields a margin for every direction in the moment space and the probability of violating the requirement. The design loop thereby informed whether a configuration provides sufficient control authority, on which axes it falls short, and how this changes with the design variables. The approach is demonstrated on a DEP regional aircraft, where the signal is used to assess the size of the vertical tail.

title: Identification and Inference of Bi-directional Causal Effects in Mendelian Randomization without Instrument Selection
summary: Mendelian randomization (MR) uses genetic variants as instruments to estimate causal effects. Bidirectional MR usually uses two reversed unidirectional analyses, but feedback can invalidate instruments in at least one direction and induce correlated pleiotropy. We model both traits as a stable cyclic system and estimate both directional effects from GWAS summary data without instrument selection or a prespecified valid-instrument subset. After LD score normalisation, marginal associations form a heteroscedastic noisy independent component analysis model, assuming the variants' direct effects on the two traits are independent. If those effects are non-Gaussian, this identifies the total-effect matrix up to scaling and permutation; no-self-feedback and stability of the system further resolve these ambiguities. We develop an estimator based on noise-adjusted second- and fourth-order moments, avoiding inversion of the high-dimensional linkage disequilibrium matrix and having computational cost linear in the number of variants. Under weak local dependence, we establish consistency, asymptotic normality, and validity of a chromosome-respecting moving block bootstrap. Simulations show negligible bias, generally reliable interval coverage, and higher rejection rates for nonzero directional effects than focusing-based tests. Three real-data applications illustrate how joint analysis of feedback systems can yield causal decompositions differing from two separate unidirectional analyses.

title: Poetry 'resurrection' from LLMs
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures, to be published in ISEA 2026 conference proceedings
summary: In an era where linguistic creativity is challenged by algorithmic authorship, we pose a provocative question: can artificial intelligence (AI) write an infinite poem? We set up two experiments to investigate the quantitative and qualitative output produced by AI utilizing couplets that evidence a poetic relationship between end words, the only variation in a strict anaphoric, litany structure. Our results show that while AI can generate interesting pairings, it still falls short of human-level creativity and understanding of poetic relationships. We offer commentary and a brief survey of the field of computational poetry experiments, tracing back authorial intention and distinctions of 'natural' and 'artificial' poetry, as well as justifying why couplet form is suited to testing AI's poetic output. Experiment 1 relies on manual prompting and co-creation to extend the original poem, which is developed into an animated webpage installation and interactive artwork. Experiment 2 reliably achieves automated output reaching the 1000 benchmark via an alternative method of using an LLM in combination with semantic similarity, of which Method 2 demonstrates a higher capacity for semantic and quantitative poetic output. These experiments highlight the limitations of current LLMs' generation capacity at the word level but also suggest that poetry will also respond and revive by incorporating AI workflows.

title: Reproduction of Simulated Acoustics Scenes Using Acoustics Room Transformer for speech intelligibility tests in Clinics
comment: This paper is submitted to Acta Acustica and is currently under review
summary: An Acoustic Room Transformation (ART) method is proposed for clinical applications to render simulated acoustic environments using six loudspeakers in a reverberant room. In typical clinical settings, testing rooms are not acoustically treated and only a limited number of loudspeakers are available. The ART approach enables control of the playback-room reverberation, allowing speech intelligibility tests to be performed under realistic and perceptually compensated conditions. The method focuses on the two most common Speech Reception Threshold (SRT) configurations: S0N90 and S0N90. One front and one side loudspeaker reproduce the direct sound components, while the remaining four loudspeakers (two in front and two behind the listener) generate the reverberant sound field. The direct sound is optimized in terms of energy, and the reverberant field is adjusted based on both energy and interaural coherence. An additional direct-sound gain is applied to match the clarity index (C50) of the reproduced signals to that of the reference target. Results from speech intelligibility tests demonstrate that, with ART processing, the reproduced scenarios achieve SRT values very close to those of the reference signal in both S0N0 and S0N90 conditions and therefore allow for comparable speech test results independent of the particular test room acoustics.

title: Quantifying Dependence Effects on $k$-out-of-$n$ Reliability Relative to the Independent Benchmark
summary: Understanding how dependence among component lifetimes affects the reliability of redundant systems is a central problem in reliability engineering. In this paper, we develop a framework for quantifying the impact of multivariate dependence on $k$-out-of-$n$ system reliability relative to the independent benchmark. Using an orthogonal Legendre expansion of the copula density, we derive an exact decomposition that separates the dependence structure from the system architecture. This representation identifies how individual dependence contributions are transmitted to system reliability through explicit structural weights. An application to multivariate Farlie-Gumbel-Morgenstern copulas demonstrates that higher-order dependence can produce distinct reliability effects even when all bivariate copulas remain unchanged. Our findings provide a systematic approach to quantifying and interpreting the effects of multivariate dependence on the reliability of redundant systems.

title: Use-case-driven ontology modeling with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living
summary: Research on smart homes and ambient assisted living (AAL) has grown steadily over the last decade, driven largely by the ageing of the population. A smart home has to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects in order to offer services tailored to its dwellers, and this requires a shared formal description of both the dwellers and the devices. We present the ontology developed as the semantic data layer of the Virtual Home Framework in the Italian Design For All project. Its requirements are derived from two use cases: a frail elderly woman who exercises at home on a cycle-ergometer, and a designer who configures a kitchen for users with different impairments. The requirements are collected in an Ontology Requirements Specification Document and the ontology is built with the NeOn methodology, reusing and reengineering existing ontologies where possible. The resulting modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and through their cardiorespiratory fitness; it also describes smart objects, their programs, the measurements they produce, and the comfort dimensions of the home. SWRL rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and identify the smart objects suited to a given impairment.

title: Dynamic Structural Causal Models for Delay Prediction
comment: Accepted in IEEE International Conference on Machine Learning for Communication and Networking (ICMLCN) 2026
summary: Dynamic network key performance indicators (KPIs) such as end-to-end (E2E) delay are shaped by both contemporaneous interactions and temporal persistence. While standard predictors can forecast KPIs under a fixed regime, proactive network management requires reasoning about the effects of explicit actions (interventions) and, in time series, executing a model forward over multiple horizons. We study dynamic structural causal models (DSCMs) for E2E delay in a 5G measurement campaign, where payload and background traffic are intentionally manipulated and thus treated as do-interventions. We learn DSCM scaffolds using four time-series causal discovery methods representing score-based and constraint-based paradigms and common lag-based baselines. Using gradient-boosted decision trees, we evaluate true multi-step DSCM rollout, which recursively simulates the full system state, and a direct target-only ablation that predicts the KPI without recursive simulation. Across two held-out intervention scenarios, including high payload and 10 Mbps background traffic, we find that the inferred target parent/lag sets differ substantially across methods and that rollout behavior is strongly scenario-dependent. In particular, PCMCI+ achieves the best short-horizon rollout accuracy under the payload intervention (RMSE 2.97~ms) but exhibits pronounced horizon-dependent degradation under the background-traffic intervention (root mean squared error (RMSE) ~4.75 ms for long horizon), yielding a large positive rollout tax of up to ~0.78 ms relative to direct prediction; DyNoTEARS and VAR-based DSCMs remain comparatively stable under rollout. These results highlight that evaluating causal scaffolds only via direct prediction can be misleading, and therefore, executability under intervention and long-horizon error propagation are critical for DSCM-based KPI reasoning.

title: Asymptotic properties for weak Markov-switching AR(p) models
summary: In this paper we study the asymptotic properties of an autoregressive model of order p (AR for short), possibly non-centered, whose parameters switch according to an unobserved Markov chain. Departing from the conventional assumption of independent innovations, we merely require the errors to be uncorrelated but not necessarily independent, thereby widening substantially the range of potential applications of Markov-switching AR models. We establish sufficient conditions for the consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed moment estimators. We also propose a consistent estimator of the asymptotic variance matrix of the moment estimators. The finite-sample performance of the proposed procedures is illustrated through Monte Carlo experiments and an empirical study based on hourly meteorological data, which together provide strong support for the theoretical findings.

title: Improved Regret via Variance-Aware Policy Optimization in Adversarial MDPs
summary: We study episodic adversarial MDPs with unknown dynamics and full-information rewards and achieve regret with leading term $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3SAK})$. Here $H$ is the horizon, $S$ the total number of states across decision layers, $A$ the number of actions, and $K$ the number of episodes. This improves the two incomparable prior leading terms by factors $\sqrt{S/H}$ and $\sqrt{H^3}$, leaving a factor $\sqrt H$ to the lower-bound scale. We give a reduction from unknown to known dynamics for \emph{downstream-dependent} algorithms, whose policy at step $h$ is computed only from information at steps $h+1$ and onward. This reduces the remaining leading-order gap to finding a downstream-dependent known-dynamics algorithm with $\widetilde O(H\sqrt K)$ regret, which would yield the tight $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{SAK})$ leading term for unknown dynamics. We instantiate the reduction with VOPO, a policy optimization (PO) algorithm. Its improved guarantees follow from a variance-aware analysis enabled by a novel bonus, which we call the Stability-Matching Bonus (SMB). VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3K})$ regret under known dynamics with full information; its $\sqrt H$ gap to the target $H\sqrt K$ rate is inherited by our unknown-dynamics guarantee. We also show that with known dynamics and trajectory bandit feedback, VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^2SAK})$ regret. Both known-dynamics guarantees improve the corresponding state-of-the-art PO bounds by a factor $\sqrt H$. A matching lower bound establishes that the full-information rate is tight in one parameter regime.

title: Channel Prediction Using Deep Recurrent Neural Network with EVT-based Adaptive Quantile Loss Function
comment: Published in: IEEE Communications Letters ( Volume: 29, Issue: 7, July 2025)
summary: Ultra-reliable low latency communication (URLLC) systems are pivotal for applications demanding high reliability and low latency, such as autonomous vehicles. In such contexts, channel prediction becomes essential to maintaining communication quality, as it allows the system to anticipate and mitigate the effects of fast-fading channels, thereby reducing the risk of packet loss and latency spikes. This letter presents a novel framework that integrates neural networks with extreme value theory (EVT) to enhance channel prediction, focusing on predicting extreme channel events that challenge URLLC performance. We propose an EVT-based adaptive quantile loss function that integrates EVT into the loss function of the deep recurrent neural networks (DRNNs) with gated recurrent units (GRUs) to predict extreme channel conditions efficiently. The numerical results indicate that the proposed GRU model, utilizing the EVT-based adaptive quantile loss function, significantly outperforms the traditional GRU. It predicts a tail portion of 7.26%, which closely aligns with the empirical 7.49%, while the traditional GRU model only predicts 2.4%. This demonstrates the superior capability of the proposed model in capturing tail values that are critical for URLLC systems.

title: Lipschitz-Constrained Discriminators in Generative Modeling: Asymptotic Behavior and Support Mismatch
summary: We study the asymptotic behavior of optimal discriminators associated to $L-$Lipschitz regularized KL-divergences of two probability distributions $Q$ and $P$ that interpolate between the rescaled Wasserstein$-1$ metric by some parameter $L>0$ and the KL divergence. The parameter $L$ plays the role of a Lipschitz constraint and is viewed as a regularization parameter: small values of $L$ enforce a more geometry-aware discriminator, while as $L$ increases the geometric regularization is progressively relaxed. It is a known result [3] that such divergences converge to the KL divergence as $L\to\infty$. In this paper, we characterize the asymptotic behavior of the optimal discriminators as $L\to\infty$ in different regimes: Firstly, under $Q\ll P$ and the Radon-Nikodym derivative $\frac{dQ}{dP}$ is bounded from above and bounded away from zero. Secondly, when $Q$ and $P$ are discrete distributions satisfying $Q\ll P$, and finally when $Q$ and $P$ are non absolutely continuous discrete distributions. This result motivates training strategies which involve discriminators, such as adversarial generative models. In practice, the data distribution is often represented by a discrete empirical measure, while, especially at the early stages of the training, the model distribution may have little or no overlap with the empirical data distribution.

title: Do Mixture-of-Experts Routers Benefit from Ensembling?
summary: Ensembles of neural networks have repeatedly been shown to outperform single networks. Ensemble theory attributes this gain to the accuracy of the individual members and the diversity among them. Mixture-of-experts models already combine many experts, but a single router decides how the experts are weighted for each input. Motivated by ensemble theory, we apply ensembling to the routing step: an ensemble of routers, trained jointly with the experts, proposes the expert weights. We systematically evaluate this approach using underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks. We analyse each experiment with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble, which, to our knowledge, has not previously been developed for routers. We report four findings. First, more routers lower the validation loss. Second, training routers to explicitly maximize expert diversity improves the mean performance on three of the four tasks. Third, explicitly maximizing router diversity has no effect on performance. Fourth, combining router weights with the arithmetic mean works better than combining them with the geometric mean. Routing benefits mildly from ensembling, but this benefit is offset by the computational cost of training additional routers.

title: Linear Dynamic Range Extension for Rydberg Atomic Receiver via Band-Limited Reconstruction
summary: Rydberg-atom receiver offers a promising approach to radio-frequency (RF) signal reception in wireless communication and sensing systems, combining high sensitivity with the potential for broad frequency coverage. However, the limited linear dynamic range (LDR) of the atomic system causes nonlinear distortion at high input signal levels, thereby restricting the receiver's effective linear input range. To address this issue, we analyze the mechanisms underlying nonlinear distortion in Rydberg atomic receivers and propose a physics-informed band-limited iterative reconstruction (PI-BLIR) method. Specifically, by exploiting the known nonlinear atomic response and signal bandwidth prior, we formulate a constrained maximum-likelihood problem to reconstruct the distorted complex intermediate-frequency (IF) waveform. With the bandwidth constraint absorbed into the frequency-domain parameterization, the constrained maximum-likelihood problem is transformed into an unconstrained optimization problem, which is solved using gradient descent. The proposed method relies solely on digital post-processing and requires no changes to the local-oscillator (LO) field strength, optical parameters, or atomic operating conditions. Simulation results demonstrate that PI-BLIR extends the receiver's LDR by more than 14 dB and enhances the demodulation performance of the atomic receiver.

title: Comments on: `CliPS: How to identify cluster distributions in Bayesian mixture models'
comment: This is an invited discussion for the paper arXiv:2603.00277v2. The citation of the published version is Malsiner-Walli, G., Frühwirth-Schnatter, S. & Grün, B. CliPS: How to identify cluster distributions in Bayesian mixture models. TEST (2026). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11749-026-01034-7
summary: I congratulate the authors on their contribution, which addresses important challenges in understanding posterior distributions in Bayesian mixture models. As underlined by the authors, the Bayesian framework has several advantages, yet label-switching, identifiability issues, and the trans-dimensional nature of parameter spaces make exploiting the Bayesian approach and understanding the resulting posterior difficult in practice. The paper offers clear explanations and a simple, intuitive procedure to address this by clustering the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws of component-specific parameters. It is clearly illustrated on several examples.

title: ERGo: Energy-Efficient Hybrid Graph Neural Network Training on Processing-In-Memory Architectures
comment: Accepted for Publication in IEEE/ACM Embedded Systems Week (ESWEEK-25)
summary: Processing-in-memory (PIM) has been proposed as an alternative computing paradigm for training Deep Neural Networks, including Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Despite these advancements, training GNN workloads on PIM devices necessitates off-chip memory access. This off-chip access is expensive in terms of performance and energy, thereby impacting the overall energy efficiency of the training process on PIM platforms. In this paper, we propose a novel hybrid training framework called ERGo that automatically switches from a full-parameter phase to a parameter-efficient phase during the training process with negligible loss in predictive accuracy. The parameter-efficient phase employs low-rank representations of GNN weights, effectively reducing the number of trainable parameters. This helps in reducing the off-chip access during the end-to-end training process on PIM architectures, leading to notable improvements in both performance and energy efficiency. ERGo outperforms the conventional full-parameter GNN training on a PIM-based platform by up to 3.15x in speedup and enhances energy efficiency by 10.5x. Furthermore, ERGo offers additional advantages when utilized on heterogeneous architectures incorporating non-volatile memory (NVM) and static random-access memory (SRAM). Training on the heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture typically utilizes NVM for the forward-pass and SRAM for the backward-pass. However, NVM cells suffer from low device endurance and repeated write operations due to weight updates can lead to poor lifetime. ERGo improves the lifetime of NVM devices by freezing the weights and preventing weight updates in the parameter-efficient phase. Experimental results demonstrate that ERGo improves the lifetime of heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture by up to 33x in comparison to full-parameter implementation.

title: PTMTD: A Topology-Aware Temporal-Graph Attention Network for Joint Cyber-Attack Detection and Relay-Level Localization in Power System Protection Networks
summary: The digitization of protection relays exposes power grids to sophisticated cyberattacks, yet existing GNN detectors omit temporal encoding, rely on static topologies, and lack relay localization. We propose PTMTD-a Pearson-driven Temporal Multimodal Topology-aware Detection Network-coupling a dilated TCN with multi-head GATv2 in a dual-head architecture for simultaneous 37-class detection and four-relay localization. PTMTD constructs its graph from measurement correlations (no impedance data) and is trained with a composite loss jointly optimizing both tasks. On the MSU-ORNL benchmark (78,377 samples, 37 classes), it achieves 99.27% accuracy, 99.25% macro F1, and 95.98% localization, outperforming GraphKAN, LSTM, GCN, and Random Forest by 5.64-11.15 percentage points (p < 0.05). Ablations confirm gains from temporal encoding (+2.38%), graph attention (+2.69%), residuals (+2.07%), and correlation-driven supervision. With 639k parameters and 2.5 ms CPU inference, PTMTD is lightweight and deployment-ready. While validated on a transmission testbed, the architecture applies to microgrids with similar relay structures. Code and models are publicly available.

title: Making Experiment Results Comparable through Sitewide Impact Estimation
comment: Extended abstract accepted for presentation at the 2026 Conference on Digital Experimentation at MIT (CODE@MIT)
summary: Roblox spans many product surfaces-discovery, the virtual economy, creator tools-that differ sharply in reach and in how much the affected population contributes to any sitewide metric. A randomized experiment shows whether a treatment works for the users in its sample, but this experiment lift is not comparable across surfaces, because surfaces differ in reach and in their contribution to sitewide metrics. The quantity a strategic decision needs is a counterfactual-how much an aggregated sitewide metric (e.g., total platform play time) would move if the treatment reached 100% of its target population, which may be only part of the sitewide population, during the measurement period. We call this sitewide impact. Its scaling factor, which we call the coverage factor, combines the reach and the target population's contribution to the sitewide metric under no treatment. Hence a low-reach surface whose users carry much of the metric could outrank a high-reach surface whose users carry little. We develop two estimators under this framing: one for difference-in-means metrics and one for variant-level ratio metrics (a metric defined as a ratio of two population aggregates). Empirically, experiment lift is a poor proxy for sitewide impact-across 139 experiments that are statistically significant on time spent, the Spearman rank correlation between the two is 0.20, and 5 of the 10 largest experiment lifts are among the 10 largest sitewide impacts. We validate the estimator with A/A tests and against a long-term holdout, and apply it to cross-domain prioritization and attributing year-over-year growth to shipped innovations.

title: Data-Driven Sparse Identification and Robust Tube-Based Predictive Control for Multivariable Chaotic Systems
summary: This paper addresses the data-driven synchronization and robust control of multivariable chaotic systems subject to strict actuation constraints, modeling uncertainties and bounded input disturbances. Using empirical data collected from a four-dimensional chaotic Rossler response system, Sequentially Thresholded Least Squares (STLSQ) sparse regression is employed to recover a nominal control-affine model, achieving an identification accuracy of R^2 = 1.0000 across all channels with root-mean-square error within [4.15e-6, 8.33e-4]. To establish a mathematically rigorous bridge between data-driven identification and robust synthesis, all structural discrepancies in the drift vector field and input matrix are unified into a single lumped uncertainty field delta(x,u). A computable scalar bound delta_bar is established based on library truncation error, regression residuals, input bounds, and Lipschitz constants (Lemma 1). We subsequently prove that input-output feedback linearization maps delta(x,u) into a state- and control-dependent additive disturbance d(z,nu) in Brunovsky canonical coordinates, bounded by ||d(z,nu)||_2 <= alpha_1 delta_bar + alpha_2 delta_bar ||nu||_2 with closed-form expressions for alpha_1 and alpha_2 (Theorem 1). This certified bound, together with a bounded input disturbance and a zero-order-hold margin, yields a compact disturbance set that seeds a robust tube-based model predictive controller. We prove that the resulting tightened quadratic program is recursively feasible, that the physical actuator limit (|u_i| <= 1100) remains inactive under an explicit sufficient condition, and that the closed-loop tracking error is Input-to-State Stable (ISS) with an asymptotic gain that is linear in delta_bar plus a term due to the exogenous input disturbance (Theorems 2 and 3).

title: A fast and sound algorithm to simplify summations in interventional queries expressions
summary: Identification formulas returned by the ID algorithm often contain summations that can be removed. The procedure proposed in arxiv:1806.07082 (TK) removes them by combining factors of the formula into joint distributions, through the chain rule and through the insertion of factors for missing variables. We make two changes to this procedure: only the factors that involve the summed variable are combined, and every factor is written with a minimal conditioning set. These two changes determine the rest of the procedure, in which each search over a power set is replaced by a single test and the variables to insert are fixed in advance, and they remove summations that the TK procedure leaves in place. The resulting procedure is sound and, for minimal input terms, complete for each individual elimination with respect to joins and insertions.
