We also carry out non-asymptotic analysis to derive the iteration complexity for the proposed FPLL to achieve the $ε$-Pareto stationary point. Extensive experiments have been undertaken to elucidate the superior efficacy of the proposed method.

title: Towards High-Performance Multimodal Discovery: Evaluating Retrieval Efficacy and Operational Scalability in Digital Libraries
summary: Large-scale digital repositories with million plus digitized volumes serve as vital engines for scientific and scholarly discovery. However, as collections grow, finding specific research or educational material remains a significant challenge. This difficulty is compounded by the multimodal nature of texts, that is, texts which combine dense narrative content with essential illustrative charts, annotated diagrams, and complex layouts. Historically, discovery has been supported by full-text search indexes implemented as inverted indexes (e.g., Lucene or Solr). While these systems scale well for textual strings, they are fundamentally "blind" to the semantic nuance of visual information. We explore the benefit of discovery through texts that have been converted to numerical vectors. By representing page images as numerical vectors rather than OCR-extracted text, and doing so for both text and images on a page, we capture both textual and visual semantics while mitigating reverse engineering and copyright infringement concerns. The primary contribution of this research is an evaluation of the multimodal retrieval landscape, encompassing both semantic precision and architectural scalability. Our findings demonstrate that integrating visual and textual features significantly enhances the discovery of relevant material, particularly in domains where diagrammatic content is essential for conceptual understanding. We assess retrieval efficacy, demonstrating that the system achieves sub-linear scalability. Our findings suggest that an optimized vector database configuration is the critical factor in transforming VLM-based embeddings into a production-ready, library-scale discovery solution.

title: A Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization in Model Merging
summary: Model merging constructs multi-task models without expensive joint training but often suffers from parameter interference. Some solutions mitigate this by constraining finetuning using data from the other tasks to be merged, violating the core independence and privacy assumption of model merging. Recent work offers preliminary empirical evidence that a universal, task-agnostic proxy distribution can substitute for such data, but leaves open when and why it suffices. To this end, we propose a \textit{Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization}, which characterizes the relationship between a proxy distribution and the distribution of other tasks to be merged through spectral coverage ($α$) and leakage ($β$). Based on the framework, we derive a unified parameter interference bound: smaller $(α, β)$ provably yields lower parameter interference through better spectral alignment. To exploit such a proxy, we augment the training objective with a proxy regularizer. Evaluating this regularizer during fine-tuning requires a concrete mechanism. We study three instantiations, including (J) an exact evaluation via Jacobian-vector products, (F) a frozen curvature approximation using the Fisher information matrix, and (O) an output-drift formulation that constrains the model's functional deviation on the proxy directly. We prove that all three coincide under the NTK linearization, where existing analyses of such regularizers stop, and go further to characterize standard non-linear fine-tuning, bounding how far each instantiation departs from its linearized reference and obtain a three-way hierarchy, zero for (J), proxy-independent for (F), and proxy-quality-scaling for (O). Empirical validation on the commonly used vision-language model CLIP confirms these theoretical predictions.

title: ERA: Error-Resistant Autonomous Object Navigation with Predicted Depth
summary: Depth and 3D foundation models can predict geometry from RGB images, allowing zero-shot object navigation without a depth sensor. However, when predicted depth is mapped as if it came from a sensor, view-dependent errors accumulate in the map, remove exploration goals, and end the search before the agent can observe and correct them. We propose ERA, a training-free object navigation system that replaces the depth sensor with depth predicted from RGB images and poses. ERA follows a paradigm we call Move with Error: movement provides new views that correct map errors, and the corrected map enables further movement. It realizes this paradigm with revisable occupancy and with exploration from reachable viewpoints, which continues the search when no frontier remains, and verifies the target across views before stopping. On three benchmarks, ERA achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods without depth sensors. Its map and exploration components also raise VLFM's success from 10.8% to 61.7% under the same predicted depth. We further deploy ERA on a real robot.

title: HarmonyText: Harmonious Scene Text Editing via Reverse-to-Refined Pair Synthesis and Region-Decoupled Frequency Learning
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures. Accepted to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers
summary: Natural language-guided, mask-free scene text editing aims to modify text in real-world images using only textual instructions, yet remains challenged by unreliable pseudo-GT supervision, over-smoothed text generation, and the absence of GT-free evaluation. Existing methods often rely on imperfect pseudo-targets with background discrepancies, while standard MSE-based velocity regression tends to suppress high-frequency details, leading to blurred text boundaries and weakened local textures. To address these issues, we propose HarmonyText, a mask-free scene text editing framework with region- and frequency-aware supervision. HarmonyText introduces Region-Decoupling Optimization (RDO), which aligns edited text regions with pseudo-targets while anchoring preserved regions to the source image, and Cascaded High-Frequency Texture Guidance (CHFTG), which applies cascaded wavelet-domain constraints to preserve sharp boundaries and fine-grained textures of textual content. We further propose Reverse-to-Refined Pair Synthesis (RePair) to construct STE25K, a high-quality 25K paired dataset, and introduce a GT-free evaluation protocol with Color Distribution Divergence and a Harmony Assessment Model. Extensive experiments show that HarmonyText outperforms existing methods in text editing accuracy, background fidelity, color consistency, and perceptual harmony.

title: Logically Consistent Accurate Forecasts
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Temporal Systems (FMTS)
summary: Agentic forecasting systems based on large language models (LLMs) are now competitive with expert human forecasters, but these systems still suffer from a critical limitation: the inability to produce forecasts that are logically consistent. For example, forecasts for related events often fail to satisfy the axioms of probability, which in turn implies that related forecasts cannot simultaneously be correct and undermines their utility for decision makers. Enforcing consistency is not trivial -- naive approaches (e.g., projection onto the set of consistent forecasts) can degrade accuracy. We argue that the key to overcoming the apparent tradeoff between consistency and accuracy lies in the reasoning which supports each forecast. We finetune a supervisory language model that leverages this reasoning to jointly reconcile inconsistencies while improving the accuracy of related forecasts. On ForecastBench, our method improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% while reducing measures of structural inconsistency by 82-90%. We interrogate our method via a comprehensive series of baselines and ablations, and find that no alternative method matches our gains in consistency and accuracy simultaneously.

title: Super-Analysis for Aggressive yet Scalable Compiler Optimization
summary:
Aggressive compiler optimization today occupies two distant extremes. Conventional optimizers run in milliseconds but reason through ad-hoc heuristics that miss opportunities; superoptimizers synthesize faster code but take hours, confining them to small kernels and offline use. We introduce solver-based super-analysis, a middle ground that uses expensive SMT-based analysis while transformations remain conventional, avoiding program synthesis entirely. The key argument for super-analysis is that conventional compilers have rich transformation rules, but proving them to be safe requires complex reasoning: proving a safety check dead often needs facts from three independent LLVM analyses simultaneously, a conjunctive entailment problem suited to an SMT solver, not to any single dataflow pass.
  We instantiate super-analysis in ODeSSy, an LLVM pass that proves sanitizer traps and native-language safety checks unreachable and removes them. One mechanism serves four frontend languages and yields speedups in each, including a 3.78x speedup for a GEMM implemented in Julia. A further solver-based optimization, guard synthesis, handles checks that are not dead for every input: the solver synthesizes a cheap invariant safety guard under which a fast check-free loop is cloned, speeding up a Swift Base64 encoder by 1.44x and a Julia LZ77 compressor by 4.01x. Compared with Souper, the synthesizing superoptimizer for LLVM, ODeSSy removes more safety checks in significantly less time, making it viable as an online compiler pass.

title: Analysing Busy Beaver Machines (Or How to Find Ossified Ocelots)
summary: The busy beaver problem involves working with machines which can produce very large numbers, both for the output of certain Turing machines and for the number of steps taken to execute them. Given that these numbers can involve thousands of digits, it is crucial to have a means of proving properties of the relevant machines which allow manipulation of such large numbers. In this paper we introduce the notion of \textit{shape computations} as a means of isolating key properties that allow efficient execution of the relevant Turing machines based on verifiable properties of state transitions. In particular, this notion allows us to provide an analytical result which demonstrates the quadratic relationship between the size of the output and the number of steps required to generate it. We have also developed an initial implementation of our approach, and we provide empirical evaluation of it on a suite of 240 example machines.

title: Evaluating the Robustness of PRNU Source-Camera Attribution to the Fingerprint-Copy Attack: An Open Toolkit with Triangle-Test Detection
summary: Photo-Response Non-Uniformity (PRNU) is the de facto standard trace for sensor-level source-camera attribution, and a high Peak-to-Correlation-Energy (PCE) between a questioned image and a camera reference fingerprint is routinely treated as strong evidence of common origin. The fingerprint-copy attack of Goljan, Fridrich and Chen (2011) shows that this signal can be forged: an adversary who estimates a target camera's fingerprint from that camera's publicly available images can inject a scaled copy of it into an unrelated photograph, producing a forgery that clears a PCE decision threshold despite never having been taken by the target device. We present prnucf, an open, auditable toolkit that pairs a reference implementation of the (additive) fingerprint-copy attack with the triangle-test detector and a cohort-calibrated decision procedure, so that practitioners can quantify how fragile a PRNU attribution is against this attack on their own pipelines. On a controlled multi-camera Monte-Carlo benchmark the attack reaches an arbitrary target PCE at a mean PSNR of 59.2 dB (visually lossless), yet the triangle test separates forgeries from innocent images with an area under the ROC curve of 0.999, detecting every forgery at a cohort-calibrated 5% false-positive operating point. We discuss why a fixed significance cut-off is not safe in casework, the limitations of synthetic validation, and the open problem of extending explainable detection to the modern, GAN-based generation of fingerprint-transfer attacks. The toolkit is released under the MIT license with an explicit dual-use statement.

title: When Does Cross-View Consistency Matter in Multi-View Appearance Augmentation? A Controlled Study for Visuomotor Policies
summary: Multi-view visual augmentation often seeks consistency across cameras, but it is unclear which forms of consistency matter for downstream control. We use simulation-state replay to manipulate cross-view coupling while preserving the per-camera perturbation distributions, physical trajectories, and action labels. Across seven LIBERO manipulation tasks, marginal-matched changes in global appearance, ghost injection, and target color have small average costs for a late-fusion Diffusion Policy: point estimates are near zero or negative, and the largest upper endpoint of the 90% posterior credible intervals is 2.55 percentage points. In contrast, geometrically anti-coupled observations reduce success by 3.30 percentage points relative to coupled observations (90% CrI [0.64, 6.28]), with displacement magnitude, direction marginals, and the number of affected views matched. Camera interventions reveal substantial dependence on wrist-view geometry, while feature analysis shows appearance sensitivity patterns associated with the factors randomized during training. ACT shows a higher target-color cost estimate than DP, with uncertainty that includes zero and sensitivity to task composition. Within the tested tasks and policy configurations, these findings motivate selective consistency constraints: appearance coupling can sometimes be relaxed, whereas task-relevant geometry and cross-view spatial correspondence warrant protection.

title: Stage-wise Lineage-aware Dropout for Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures, 7 tables, including supplementary material
summary: Sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is prone to overfitting because only a limited number of images are available to constrain scene geometry. Dropout is one regularization strategy for alleviating this problem. We introduce the concept of a lineage family to describe a set of Gaussian primitives derived from the same founder through cloning or splitting operations. The founder Gaussians refer to all Gaussian primitives generated during initialization. Descendants within the same family often jointly contribute to the refinement of adjacent local regions. However, dropping individual Gaussians can be less effective due to the compensation effect from neighboring Gaussians for the dropped ones. To address this issue, we propose Stage-wise Lineage-aware Dropout(SLD), which applies lineage-family dropout during the structural regularization stage and switches to individual dropout during the later refinement stage. We further propose Lineage-Balanced Densification(LBD), which operates during densification by constructing an expanded candidate pool and reallocating the densification budget according to the mean gradient scores and existing descendant sizes of different families. Experiments on the LLFF, MipNeRF360, and Blender datasets show that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance in sparse-view reconstruction

title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
summary: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. For Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working receives its first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama, and mlx_lm.server. On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at https://github.com/basecompute/superfluid.

title: See Every Block Once: Variance-Reduced Post-Training for Masked Diffusion Language Models
summary: Policy gradient methods are widely used to align large language model outputs with human preferences, but the log-likelihoods they require cannot be directly computed in Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs). MDLM post-training therefore relies on a surrogate objective based on the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), and recent work estimates a blockwise variant of this objective via Monte Carlo methods to support blockwise generation. However, existing estimation schemes randomly sample the block index, so they may evaluate the same block more than once and leave some blocks unevaluated. This introduces variance arising from block selection into the estimates. In this work, we propose a full-block estimator that evaluates every block exactly once and averages the results. We theoretically show that the proposed estimator remains unbiased while eliminating the between-group variance arising from block selection, thereby achieving lower variance than the baseline for the same sample size. In experiments on five benchmarks spanning mathematics, planning, and coding, our method achieves the highest accuracy on four benchmarks and outperforms the random block sampling baseline by an average of 12.79 points.

title: VACO: Vertex-Aligned Decoding for Dense Hand Contact Estimation from a Single Image
summary: Dense hand contact estimation from a single RGB image is a foundational primitive for dexterous manipulation and 3D interaction analysis. Direct predictors typically decode the entire per-vertex contact map from one shared query, leaving individual vertices ungrounded in the image and smearing contact across adjacent, non-touching surfaces. We present VACO, a vertex-aligned decoder in which each MANO vertex samples local image features at its projected location. A hand-reconstruction backbone, jointly trained for reconstruction and contact, predicts these locations at inference without an auxiliary reconstructor. Training uses noise-perturbed ground-truth projections and end-to-end feature adaptation to improve robustness and contact-sensitive features. A single VACO checkpoint sets a new state of the art on five benchmarks spanning hand-object, hand-human, hand-scene, and bimanual interactions. It improves F1 by +20.7 pp over the strongest prior direct predictor on Hi4D and generalizes to the held-out HOT3D and HOCap, with gains of +5.5 and +2.7 pp. The resulting contact predictions also improve downstream HOI reconstruction.

title: Compiling Matrix Formulas to Quantum Block Encodings
summary:
Realizing the promise of quantum applications such as chemistry or fluid dynamics requires building quantum circuits that efficiently encode and manipulate exponentially large matrices. This process forces researchers to grapple with the reality that a matrix expressible as one equation on paper can map to thousands of bit-level quantum logic gates, historically written by hand. Even worse, it often ends with a discovery that the needed resources grow so quickly with matrix size that the quantum algorithm loses its asymptotic speedup.
  In this work, we present MARBLE, a language that automatically synthesizes an efficient circuit from the publication-style formula for the entries of a matrix. MARBLE algebraically rewrites programs into symbolic combinations of simpler matrices that have known circuit realizations. It analyzes costs of possible representations, notably the subnormalization term that dominates time complexity. It then emits an OpenQASM circuit and certifies whether its cost is poly-logarithmic in problem size, as required by quantum algorithms.
  When evaluated on quantum applications ranging from fluid dynamics to physical Hamiltonians, MARBLE matches or surpasses 37 of 39 published baselines. On the low end, it automatically matches many theoretically optimal circuits, and on the high end, it improves on a published construction in fluid dynamics by 10,487x in subnormalization. MARBLE produces exponentially smaller circuits than the leading tool FABLE, and it successfully compiles matrices whose dimensions exceed 2^100 within five seconds on a laptop.

title: Efficient Genotype Classification from 3D MRI in ADPKD via Density-Aware Point Sampling and E(3)-invariance
summary: Early detection of genetic kidney diseases, especially autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), is crucial because certain genotypes such as truncating PKD1 mutations cause rapid kidney growth and early progression to end-stage kidney disease. MRI-based genotype inference is a potential low-cost complement to genetic testing. However, although many deep learning methods have been developed for classifying various MR images, applying them to ADPKD remains challenging: (1) abdominal MR images are generally too large to be handled by deep learning models designed for smaller images like brain MRI, and (2) the amount of labeled data for ADPKD genetic mutations is insufficient to train deep learning models. In order to address these challenges, we propose E3PN, an efficient 3D MRI-based ADPKD genotype classification network that relies on point sampling and E(3)-invariance. We utilize a point representation of 3D MRI, which consumes less GPU memory than a voxel representation. For further memory efficiency, 3D points are sampled from a mixture distribution over the two kidneys in each image. Since E(3)-invariance has been shown to improve data efficiency, we also incorporate it into our model through coordinate canonicalization. On our ADPKD dataset, E3PN trains 163 times faster and uses 103x less GPU memory than a 3D ResNet, while also improving F1 from 0.165 to 0.226 over both baselines. These results establish a first benchmark for five-way ADPKD genotype classification from 3D MRI and show that point sampling and coordinate canonicalization yield two-orders-of-magnitude efficiency gains with a modest but consistent improvement in F1.

title: Convergence analysis of physics-informed neural networks for subdiffusion
summary: Physics-informed neural networks have emerged as mesh-free solvers for partial differential equations, yet their rigorous convergence theory for time-fractional problems remains limited. We present a convergence analysis of PINNs for linear subdiffusion equations and for the associated backward problem of recovering the initial data from terminal observations. To address the nonlocality and weakly singular kernels of fractional derivatives, we introduce a discretization-based PINN framework built on some popular time-stepping schemes satisfying discrete maximal regularity, including backward Euler, BDF2, L1, and fractional CN schemes. This approach avoids the exact evaluation of fractional derivatives at training points while preserving the stability structure needed for convergence analysis. For the forward problem, we prove that, under the natural fractional maximal-regularity condition $u\in W^{α,p}(0,T;L^2(Ω))\cap L^p(0,T;H^2(Ω)\cap H_0^1(Ω))$, the piecewise linear temporal reconstructions of PINN-loss minimizers converge to the exact solution. This result avoids the higher-order regularity assumptions on the exact solution that are often imposed in existing PINN convergence analyses. We also verify the required discrete maximal regularity and consistency properties for the aforementioned popular time discretizations. We then extend the analysis to the backward subdiffusion problem and establish convergence of the regularized recovery of the initial data from terminal observations, despite its ill-posedness. Numerical experiments for both forward and backward problems support the theoretical results, demonstrate the necessity of regularization, and show that $L^2$-type losses alone are generally insufficient. These results establish a rigorous theoretical basis for discretization-based PINNs for time-fractional diffusion problems.

title: Creative Product Design under Brand Image Constraints
summary: Industrial design requires creative visual exploration while satisfying constraints that are often product-specific and implicit. Existing text-to-image (T2I) approaches can generate creative designs through concept blending or multi-agent self-enhancement, but they provide limited mechanisms for ensuring that generated designs remain consistent with such constraints. We focus on brand image as a representative design constraint and propose a framework for brand-aware redesign generation. Given a product name, the framework constructs a brand image survey report that summarizes product and market information, derives a creative direction from the report, and integrates this direction into a self-enhancement loop in which generated images are critiqued and prompts are revised. We evaluate the framework on 50 redesign tasks across five product categories, comparing it with Naive T2I, IP-Adapter/IT-Blender, and unconstrained self-enhancement under the same T2I backbone. By a VLM-as-Judge protocol to measure creativity and brand identifiability, the proposed framework achieves a more favorable trade-off between the two objectives, with particularly clear gains in highly constrained categories such as automotive and motorcycle, where the plausible design space is relatively limited compared with that of other product categories. These results suggest that dynamically eliciting and textualizing brand image can guide creative product design generation under brand image constraints.

title: Knowledge After Collapse: Context and Wording Shape Factual Accessibility in Language Models
summary: When a language model accepts a false correction in a factual discussion, its next answer can depend on how the conversation continues. We introduce Knowledge Answer Divergence (KAD), an event-conditioned evaluation protocol that distinguishes initial false-answer adoption from subsequent persistence, recovery, and abstention. KAD freezes the conversation at the first explicit adoption of a designated false target and branches independent probes from that exact history. This enables matched comparisons of post-adoption behavior and history-management interventions that a single susceptibility score cannot capture. We evaluate eight local checkpoint conditions and six hosted endpoints, alongside an audited 300-question rerun. In corrected Llama 3.2 Instruct 3B controls, a neutral-history branch yields 42/46 correct responses, compared with 16/46 under full history. A matched cue-placement control changes false adoption by 27.3 percentage points in Qwen 3.5 4B. Twelve independently authored pressure templates demonstrate substantial sensitivity to wording. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of KAD for evaluating factual reliability beyond initial susceptibility, enabling systematic comparisons of false-answer persistence, recovery conditions and conversational interventions.

title: Toward the Minimal Set of Information Inequalities in Regenerating Codes: An Algebraic Approach
summary: Information-theoretic outer bounds for exact-repair regenerating codes can be formulated as linear programs, but the associated Shannon-type systems contain many implicit equalities and redundant inequalities. We directly specify a reduced system for the $(n,n-1,n-1)$ exact-repair model using the closure structure induced by its repair dependencies. Nonempty closed sets index the reduced joint-entropy coordinates, and inseparable edges determine the defining inequalities. We prove equivalence with the initial system by characterizing its implicit equalities and establishing sufficient redundancy criteria. We also give an algorithm that constructs the directly defined system for any $n$, count its entropy coordinates, and derive an explicitly computable upper bound on its number of inequalities. For every $n\ge2$, we prove that the reduced system has no implicit equalities and that each distinct defining inequality is nonredundant and defines a facet in the nonempty closed-set coordinate space. Exact enumerations for $n\in\{2,3,4,5\}$ verify the reported system sizes.

title: GDP.xlsx: Benchmarking Frontier Models on Professional Workbooks
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Accepted to the Agent Evaluation Science Symposium (New York City, November 2026). Leaderboard: https://surgehq.ai/benchmarks/gdp-xlsx ; evaluation harness: https://github.com/surge-ai/gdp-xlsx ; public tasks: https://huggingface.co/datasets/surgeai/GDP.xlsx
summary: We introduce GDP_xlsx, a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with an expert rubric of binary criteria and with the complete workbook or CSV file it refers to. Together the files hold 2.18 million populated cells, and the rubrics 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, and an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric. Completeness and exclusivity criteria require set-valued answers to be found in full and with nothing extra. We rank models by strict pass@1, the share of attempts that meet every criterion. Across 20 model configurations, including frontier models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the top-scoring one, Gemini 4 Argon, passes only 38.3% of attempts, and the median score is 19.3%, leaving wide headroom. We release the evaluation harness and three public tasks; the other 67 are held out to protect the leaderboard from contamination.

title: Learning Anisotropic Prediction Targets for Flow Models
summary: Flow-based generative models are trained on a hand-chosen prediction target, such as the velocity, the noise, or the clean data. This choice strongly affects training and sample quality. We introduce Anisotropic Flow Models (AnisoFlow), which replaces a fixed prediction target with a fully learnable one. AnisoFlow learns to scale the noise component of the target anisotropically, assigning a separate nonnegative weight to each direction in a jointly learned basis. A closed-form map recovers the velocity from the network's prediction, leaving the architecture, flow-matching loss, and sampler unchanged. Since recovery is exact, training optimizes the target purely to make it easier for the network to predict. We theoretically analyze the resulting prediction error and predict that the preferred noise weight in each direction scales near-linearly with data variance, in agreement with the weights learned empirically in pixel space. AnisoFlow improves FID from 1.90 to 1.55 over the JiT baseline on ImageNet 256$\times$256, by learning only the prediction target, without representation alignment or architectural changes. In pixel-space text-to-image generation, AnisoFlow improves image quality and, through better-conditioned velocity recovery, largely removes patch-seam artifacts under reduced-precision inference.

title: Activation Steering the Nan-Shan in Typhoon
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS Creative AI Track 2026. Website: https://stormhelm.net/
summary: Typhoon is an audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella, in which Captain MacWhirr steers the steamer Nan-Shan directly into and through a catastrophic storm. The novella is a study of what happens when the scale of a phenomenon exceeds the practical and conceptual frameworks available to comprehend it and of the paralysis that sometimes follows a demand for action in such overwhelming circumstances. We chose the text of Typhoon to reflect on human culture's current AI moment. We prompt a large language model, seeded with Conrad's original language, to feed endlessly on its own output, and explore when and how the text becomes increasingly alien and unwieldy as time progresses, including deviations from the narrative, digressions into the model's own instructions and thinking, and long periods of incoherent rumination. We employ methods from activation steering, including a novel adaptive steering method we introduce, to control the rhythm of the narrative and the model's digressions over long stretches of generation. The simultaneous efficacy and unpredictability of this steering showcases the tension between the perceived interpretability of AI, and the reality of a system that remains outside our comprehension and control.

title: Bridge: Database-Grounded Interactive Disambiguation for Text-to-SQL
summary: Ambiguity remains a persistent challenge in text-to-SQL, where an underspecified natural-language question may admit multiple plausible SQL interpretations. Recent work attempts to recover the user's intended interpretation through iterative clarification, but typically relies heavily on LLM parametric knowledge for ad hoc reasoning, leading to limited ambiguity-resolution effectiveness and high LLM cost. We further observe that many ambiguity errors stem from ambiguous column grounding, which remains poorly handled. Therefore, we propose Bridge, a database-grounded disambiguation framework built on an existing iterative protocol. Bridge supplies the LLM's ambiguity detection with offline-distilled knowledge about potential ambiguity relations among columns in the target database. Offline, Bridge constructs a Column Ambiguity Graph by first identifying potentially ambiguous column pairs using complementary database-grounded signals, followed by LLM-based verification. Online, columns and values mentioned in a previous incorrect SQL prediction are used as anchors to retrieve alternatives from the Column Ambiguity Graph and an offline-constructed value similarity index, respectively. The results are integrated for further pruning and consolidated for subsequent ambiguity detection. Extensive experiments on BIRD-dev without the benchmark-provided evidence show that, at comparable LLM cost, Bridge outperforms the strongest baseline by 11.60% in execution accuracy and improves the recall and precision of column usage in the final SQL by 5.25% and 12.37%, respectively.

title: Antidistillation is Cheap: Lightweight Distillation-Resistance via Stylistic Corruption
summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a highly effective paradigm for transferring capabilities from large language models (LLMs) to smaller, more specialized student models. In commercial deployment where frontier models are restricted behind black-box APIs, sequence-level distillation remains a potent vector for competitors to clone proprietary capabilities at a fraction of the development cost. Existing defenses mostly rely on surrogate models to manipulate next-token sampling, which increases computational overhead and real-time inference latency. In this work, we propose a lightweight defense that dynamically injects style-steering vectors into the teacher model's activations upon malicious queries. This framework offers exceptional flexibility, allowing hosts to customize target defensive styles and dynamically blend them to maximize stylistic variance. Crucially, this inference-time intervention preserves semantic utility and fluency during malicious queries, misleading adversaries into believing that they are extracting pristine teacher outputs, while standard consumers continue to receive original, unmodified responses. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework successfully disrupts student learning, achieving substantial anti-distillation performance while incurring negligible overhead and preserving text naturalness. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/distill-resist-38C6/.

title: Compatible by Construction: Bottom-Up Nonlinear Model Reduction without Interface Bases
summary: Nonlinear manifolds can provide compact representations of solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs), but generating training data and learning these representations on large domains remain costly. We present a bottom-up framework that reuses local nonlinear representations learned on a small training domain to solve larger PDE systems. A shared nonlinear decoder represents the full set of degrees of freedom owned by each subdomain, without separate interior and interface models. Each global degree of freedom has a unique owner, and local residuals directly use decoded state values from the corresponding neighboring subdomains. The resulting discrete state is single-valued by construction, eliminating the need for independent interface copies and additional interface compatibility constraints. Physical coupling is retained through the original time-discrete PDE residual. With the decoder held fixed, the subdomain-specific reduced coordinates are determined jointly by minimizing this residual, and the Gauss--Newton system is assembled from local contributions. Experiments on parameterized viscous Burgers and incompressible Navier--Stokes problems demonstrate reuse on larger domains without retraining. Comparisons with local proper orthogonal decomposition models under the same coupling construction show favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-offs in the tested regimes.

title: Beyond Prediction Gain: LASR as a Metric for Action-Grounded Latents in World Models
summary: World models that support planning, control, and interpretable reasoning require latent representations that genuinely encode action. Yet the large-scale video data from which such models are learned overwhelmingly lack action annotations. Latent-action models infer action-like variables from observation sequences, enabling action-aware learning from unlabeled videos or trajectories. A fundamental concern, however, remains: a latent that improves future prediction may simply encode the current state, episode progress, task identity, or other predictive shortcuts. Existing evaluation practices---reconstruction loss, rollout fidelity, action recovery, or downstream performance---cannot isolate this distinction. We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric that measures, under offline evaluation on held-out data, whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives. LASR provides two complementary summaries: GeoLASR captures typical support, while WorstLASR identifies the weakest case. We instantiate the LASR benchmark with recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes as targets, episode-held-out splits, one predictor type for all comparisons, and positive and negative controls. Experiments on recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel demonstrate that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and enables graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. We further use LASR to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter, obtaining descriptively better point estimates whose uncertainty is assessed with paired comparisons. LASR thus provides a principled offline protocol for measuring action-related predictive support in world-model latents.

title: Certified Improvements to Best-Known Thomson-Problem Configurations with a Search Pipeline Built with Large Language Model Agents
summary: The Thomson problem asks for N unit charges on a sphere with minimum Coulomb energy; for large N the best configurations known are curated in the Cambridge Cluster Database, whose largest-N entries were set in October 2026. We report configurations for N = 912, 1382 and 2502 with energies 0.0036186, 0.0109730 and 0.0614033 below the database values, certified by exact integer arithmetic. All three are numerically strict local minima modulo rotations and keep the defect inventory and scar compositions of the database configurations; the database value for N = 912 had been reached by two different methods. Our search runs unconstrained replica-exchange basin hopping from the database configurations, with a shared pool of minima, recombination of improved regions after relabelling by geometry, and gradient-only polishing; replica-exchange basin hopping alone found the N = 912 and 1382 configurations, the former in one of five runs. We built and ran it with large language model agents (Claude, through a chat interface and the Claude Code agent), and we report every search, including those that failed. Two findings matter for others who search the database. Polishing alone lowers two entries by more than the threshold at which our pipeline reports a candidate, which produced two spurious records until candidates were compared with the polished database energies (the polished baseline). A local-relaxation speed-up passed its exactness test yet found nothing in a controlled comparison in which every arm with full relaxation went below the database value within 15 minutes. We distil three practices for computational discovery with large language model agents: calibrate the search code and verify candidates with code separate from the search, compare candidates with the polished baseline, and test design changes in controlled comparisons with pass criteria fixed in advance.

title: Mobile Edge Deployment and Resource Management for Maritime Wireless Networks
summary: Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) has been envisioned as one of the key technologies for supplying computation and storage resources in Internet of Vessels (IoV) networks. Due to its flexible deployment, low cost and agile maneuverability, Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) has emerged as a promising solution, to provide communication and computation services for maritime users. In this paper, we study mobile edge deployment and resource management for MEC-assisted maritime wireless networks where USVs with diverse computation resources are deployed to provide edge computing services that complement the cloud-based services. To this end, we formulate an optimization problem to minimize the expected response time by jointly optimizing the deployment of mobile USVs and computation offloading decisions. To solve the mixed-integer nonlinear program problem, we propose a Dual-Layer Reinforcement Learning (DLRL) framework to attain a near-optimal solution. Specifically, a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm is designed to obtain the best USV deployment in the outer layer learning, and a Q-learning algorithm is designed to determine the best computation offloading decisions in the inner layer learning. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed solution outperforms some literature algorithms by effectively handling both continuous and discrete variables.

title: LuthorSQL: A One-Pass Text-to-SQL Model as System 1 for a Slower LLM Agent
summary: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are among the most accurate text-to-SQL systems, but per-query calls to a hosted model are slow, costly, and expose sensitive organizational queries to external APIs. For example, a Claude Opus 5.5 agent serving 10,000 queries a day costs over $70,000 a year at list price. To what extent can local hardware already owned by an organization offload this burden without compromising the agent's accuracy? We present LuthorSQL, a non-autoregressive 7B text-to-SQL model that serves as a rapid System 1 gate for a slower LLM agent (System 2), escalating queries only when uncertain. LuthorSQL makes a single forward pass to predict slot scores over a bounded grammar for query plans, compiles and runs up to 32 candidate plans, and chooses an answer using a trained validator. On its own, LuthorSQL reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set at 0.84 s per question on a single GPU, maintains its accuracy in 9 GB with 8-bit quantized weights, and transfers zero-shot to Snowflake, BigQuery, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB within 3.1 points of its native SQLite accuracy. Combined with Claude Opus 5.5 in a pre-registered confidence cascade over 227 questions on databases published after Opus's training cutoff, LuthorSQL answers nearly half of all questions locally and cuts API cost by 33.3% at the same accuracy. Finally, contamination probing shows that Opus reproduces 48-92% of public benchmark gold queries verbatim without seeing the schema; however, its tool-assisted accuracy holds on renamed schemas and reaches 95.6-97.4% on post-cutoff databases. Code and data: https://github.com/IAMIbrahimmemon/luthorsql

title: TReC: Evaluating Move-Induced State Changes in Instruction-Conditioned Go
summary: When a Go model predicts a move different from the expert's, coordinate distance measures how far the prediction lands from the reference. We introduce Transition Representation Consistency (TReC) to compare how the two moves change a board-state embedding. Both moves are executed from the same position under the game rules, and TReC is the cosine similarity between the two resulting representation changes. In experiments with a frozen KataGo network on 680 mid-to-late-game positions from five games, the gap between the highest and lowest candidate per position has a median of 0.01 to 0.08 for the direct successor-state cosine and 0.88 to 1.33 for TReC, depending on the evaluator layer. TReC follows coordinate distance only weakly: the rank correlation between a candidate's distance to the reference and its TReC, computed within each position, has a median of -0.19 over these positions.

title: Direction or Magnitude? Learning Scalars over Task-Calibrated Directions
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR, which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. The combination of adaptation quality, a compact trainable state, and training efficiency makes SCALAR a promising approach to resource-constrained fine-tuning.

title: CHARMING: Parallel Edge AI Acceleration Across Tensor Processing and In-Memory Computation
summary:
Edge AI increasingly relies on specialized accelerators for low-latency inference under tight resource and energy constraints, yet their efficiency remains limited by data movement. Prior work, CHARM, mitigates this overhead by overlapping data movement with computation. We observe that in-memory computing can further supplement tensor processing as a parallel accelerator while eliminating certain data movements entirely.
  We present CHARMING, a heterogeneous edge AI architecture that uses accuracy- and quantization-aware partitioning to distribute and concurrently execute inference workloads across tensor processing and in-memory computation. CHARMING partitions attention heads between an AIE array and an in-DRAM compute unit, balancing execution according to model architecture, sequence length, and precision while selecting heads to minimize accuracy degradation. CHARMING also integrates quantization into the AIE projection stage to further reduce data movement. We validate CHARMING end-to-end in hardware on AMD Versal VCK5000 and Alveo U200 platforms and evaluate LLM and video-generation models across multiple precisions using measured hardware results and simulation of the latest in-memory compute hardware.
  CHARMING improves prefill performance by up to 23.6 percent and decode performance by up to 44 percent over AIE-only acceleration. With int4 x int4 fixed-point in-memory computation, CHARMING reduces per-layer energy by up to 7.6 percent and improves energy-delay product by up to 24.7 percent, while maintaining accuracy similar to a 32-bit floating-point baseline.

title: Towards Seconds-level Video Representation: Quadratically Gated Feature Grid with Adaptive, Prediction-free Sampling
comment: 13 pages, 11 figures, 4 tables. Code available at https://github.com/MillenRosen/Q-GAS
summary: Implicit neural video representations are notoriously slow to build, which does not cross the basic practical threshold for most industrial applications. Here, we present Q-GAS, a coordinate-queryable video representation that couples multi-resolution explicit 3D feature grids with a compact SwiGLU-style quadratic-gating (QG) decoder and an error-aware, prediction-free sampler. The explicit grids avoid hash-collision coefficient sharing at the cost of modestly higher storage yet greatly boost the expressive capacity; the QG decoder introduces low-rank local second-order interactions to improve the nonlinear feature response. During fitting, a global error map periodically refreshes a high-error pool, and each batch mixes pool samples with uniform samples, which is free from the auxiliary model to predict difficult samples, thereby further escalating the efficiency. On UVG Beauty/Bosphorus/Jockey, Q-GAS fits and quantizes under 50 s on one RTX PRO 6000, decodes at over 370 FPS with mixed precision and about 146 FPS in FP32. In our PyTorch implementation, Q-GAS trains and quantizes 5.5-7.2 times faster than the evaluated Instant-NGP baseline and 19-28 times faster than RNeRV. Under a 90 s budget, it improves PSNR/MS-SSIM/LPIPS over the evaluated NeRV-family pipelines at comparable BPP over the measured overlap. We have shared our code at https://github.com/MillenRosen/Q-GAS for readers' free use.

title: RAG-FGO: Dynamic Optimization of Query-Rewriting Agents for Generative RAG
summary: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), query rewriting serves as a core interface that aligns user intent with external knowledge bases, and its effectiveness directly determines overall system performance. However, generative retrieval faces three critical challenges in real-world deployment: noisy retrieval feedback, the difficulty of jointly optimizing discrete prompt templates and continuous decoding-control parameters, and the limited generalization of static rewriting strategies under semantically complex scenarios. To address these issues, we propose RAG-FGO, a dynamic optimization framework for generative retrieval strategies. RAG-FGO formulates query rewriting as a non-differentiable black-box optimization problem in a mixed discrete-continuous space, and represents prompt templates and decoding parameters as adaptively optimizable query-rewriting agents. The framework performs global search to enable semantic jumps and structural reorganization that escape local optima, while applying local perturbations for fine-grained alignment and precise refinement. In addition, RAG-FGO introduces an elite-preserving memory pool that accumulates high-quality strategies across iterations, thereby mitigating the impact of stochasticity and noisy feedback on optimization stability. Experimental results on a diverse suite of benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method, supporting its applicability to complex semantic retrieval tasks.

title: Can Large Language Models Optimize Pretrained Neural Network Weights? A Multi-Phase Empirical Evaluation of Gradient-Free Editing in YOLO26 Object Detection
summary: Direct weight editing offers a gradient-free alternative to fine-tuning pretrained detectors, but its generalization and the value of large language model (LLM) guidance remain uncertain. We evaluate five experimental phases using YOLO26 models and MS COCO, comparing deterministic scaling, random perturbations, differential evolution, CMA-ES, structured interventions, real local-LLM proposals, failure-aware guidance, and hybrid LLM-CMA-ES against a matched random-policy control. Optimization uses native Ultralytics mAP50-95 on 1,000 COCO Val2017 images; selected candidates are assessed on a disjoint, previously examined 1,500-image subset, with COCO API AP50-95 reported separately where available. Increasing the CMA-ES budget from 8 to 250 evaluations raised development gains from +0.11 to +0.28 percentage points, while selection changes remained negative (-0.03 to -0.12 points); the 250-evaluation result uses one seed. The hybrid LLM approach showed no statistically established advantage over random-policy guidance (p = 0.612, 0.369, and 0.694 at budgets 8, 25, and 50). Five-seed YOLO26m replication yielded a COCO API AP difference of +0.004 points (95% CI: -0.026 to +0.034). Of 225 archived LLM proposals, 53 satisfy the final strict schema; early tensor-level execution cannot be fully verified. Genuine LLM-mediated weight editing is feasible, but the tested approaches did not demonstrate consistent transfer beyond the development subset or a measurable LLM advantage.

title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL researcher. Specifically, AutoRL consists of three RL-specific agentic roles. Perceptors track training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency, triggering deliberation when they detect anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three complementary Proposers diagnose problems and refine candidate interventions through shared evidence and checks. The Orchestrator reviews their recommendation and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate the superiority of AutoRL over static RL recipes and a general agent. The research records show that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment. The difficulty for future RSI lies in developing fundamental methods that are valuable for resource-consuming validation.

title: MASTARS: Multi-Agent Sequential Trajectory Augmentation with Return-Conditioned Subgoals
summary: The performance of offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is limited by the quality of the fixed offline dataset, motivating trajectory augmentation. However, augmenting multi-agent trajectories presents a fundamental challenge of the diversity-coordination trade-off: independent generation improves diversity but lacks coordination, while joint generation induces coordination but lacks diversity, reproducing the training distribution. To address this challenge in multi-agent data augmentation, we introduce MASTARS, a novel diffusion-based framework that generates multi-agent trajectories sequentially across agents while enforcing cross-agent consistent coordination via the method of inpainting. MASTARS produces trajectories that are diverse, coordinated and globally coherent. Experiments on various benchmarks such as MPE, SMAC, and SMAC-v2 demonstrate significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL methods.

title: Federated Physics-Informed Thermal Field Prediction Across Unseen Geometries in Distributed Additive Manufacturing
summary: In additive manufacturing (AM), each change in part geometry requires a new thermal simulation, which makes design evaluation over many candidates costly. Geometry-aware models reduce this cost by predicting thermal fields on unseen parts with a single learned model, but they assume that diverse geometries are available centrally. This assumption is restrictive when each manufacturing site holds only a limited set of proprietary part designs that it cannot share. We propose Fed-PIGANO, a federated framework that trains physics-informed geometry-aware neural operator (PI-GANO) models at individual sites and aggregates their geometry encoders and prediction networks without sharing part geometries. We evaluate the framework on a 2D steady-state thermal benchmark for metal AM, with geometries from five polygonal families distributed across three sites under four scenarios that range from identical to strongly different family compositions. Over seven replications, Fed-PIGANO achieves mean relative L2 errors of 1.83% to 2.04% across all 12 scenario-site cases, compared with up to 20.46% for local-only training, and consistently yields lower PDE residuals. Its prediction accuracy is comparable to that of a centralized model trained on the pooled geometries of all sites. These results demonstrate that federated learning lets manufacturing sites benefit from each other's geometries without sharing them, enabling rapid thermal prediction on new part designs for tasks such as shape optimization, inverse design, and uncertainty quantification.

title: Robustness Evaluation of GPU Cloud Pricing Benchmarks under Incomplete Observations: A Controlled Missingness Study
summary: Daily GPU rental-price benchmarks can fail when marketplace quotes are missing. This article stress-tests a fixed equal-weight median rule under four imposed masking mechanisms and four benchmark-level recovery methods. Across 5,800 Monte Carlo realisations in 27 scenarios on 190 held-out days, whole-source outages reduce publication coverage to 0.77 while preserving zero conditional error on published dates; composition-changing loss retains 0.86 coverage but produces 7.74 log points of error. A separate past-only stratum-level ablation reduces error by 4.15 to 6.70 log points in five composition-changing cases, using a richer information set. An observable-signal withholding rule improves the primary error-coverage criterion in 0 of 10 cases. Results concern observed asking-price measurements, not transaction prices or identified real-world missingness mechanisms.

title: Vision-as-a-Tool: Visual Harness for Multimodal Agentic Coding
comment: 27 pages, including references and appendices. Project page: https://vision-as-a-tool.github.io/
summary: Multimodal agentic coding requires robust visual reasoning to analyze observations and evaluate generated artifacts. Current frameworks largely rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, where agents depend on their intrinsic vision to execute visually grounded tasks. However, this architectural coupling introduces a fundamental bottleneck. Agent performance remains strictly bounded by internal perceptual limitations. Furthermore, text-only agents lack native perception. Without specialized tools, they cannot perform visual reasoning. To overcome these constraints, we introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) paradigm. Prior visual tool-use merely manipulates images for an agent's intrinsic vision to read. In contrast, VaaT reframes general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as callable external utilities. As a result, text-only agents can completely offload visual reasoning during agentic execution. Meanwhile, vision-capable agents can dynamically augment their native perception on demand. We instantiate this paradigm in VHarness, a unified framework driven by five atomic actions. We comprehensively evaluate VHarness across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D generation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that VHarness consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy across both text-only and multimodal coding agents. These findings highlight that modularizing visual reasoning into callable utilities provides a flexible and scalable foundation for future agentic coding systems.

title: Elasticy: A Runtime-Reconfigurable Architecture for Dynamic Streams
summary:
Reconfigurable Dataflow Accelerators (RDAs) have demonstrated high performance and energy efficiency for dense, regular tensor applications. However, conventional RDAs with static configurations show dramatically reduced performance and efficiency on irregular tensor workloads with data-dependent, non-uniform, dynamic tensor shapes. We propose Elasticy, a dynamically reconfigurable dataflow accelerator that employs streaming and tile abstractions to minimize the overhead of dynamic support. By encoding dynamic shapes into streams using rank-variable expressions, Elasticy exploits data-dependent tensor shape dynamism to minimize off-chip data traffic and wasted compute cycles. Elasticy employs stream-embedded reconfiguration information to trigger fine-grained runtime scheduling decisions. Elasticy also introduces a novel distributed linked streaming memory (DLSM) that more effectively uses on-chip memory to minimize off-chip data traffic and support dynamically sized tensors.
  Both reconfiguration and shape dynamism incur minimal overhead in Elasticy: reconfiguration occurs infrequently at the granularity of a stream of tiles, while rank-variable expressions enable lightweight handling of dynamic dimensions. On a Llama 3-8B decode layer, Elasticy achieves 92.6% of its roofline performance, compared to 69.7% on an H100. On evaluated GEMMs, the DLSM reduces total off-chip traffic by up to 61.4% relative to the best evaluated cache configuration, with no additional burden of programmer-managed memory. Elasticy's distributed runtime scheduler overlaps dependent kernels, speeding up kernel pairs by up to 1.42x. Programs can also run in both space and time: each phase of a layer's graph is pipelined spatially, while phases fold onto the same fabric over time. Compared to a traditional spatial accelerator, Elasticy achieves a 6.34x-31.67x improved area delay product on full layers.

title: Multimodal Person Concept Model for Person Identification under Varying Observation Conditions
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Submitted to Artificial Life and Robotics (AROB Journal Track). Project page: https://okitamisan01.github.io/person_concept/
summary: Service robots in domestic and office environments must identify users to provide personalized services based on their preferences and previous interactions. This is challenging because only a few observations may be available for learning, while observation conditions change owing to appearance, environmental noise, and utterance content. To address this challenge, this study proposes a multimodal person concept model that learns person concepts from a small number of observations, without person labels, and enables robust identification under changing conditions. The model employs a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process and integrates visual, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted using Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) and Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP), followed by principal component analysis (PCA). We evaluated six participants under eight conditions in which appearance changes, additive noise, and transcription errors were introduced individually and in combination. Averaged over the eight conditions, the proposed model achieved an identification accuracy of 0.89 while inferring the number of person concepts from the observations, which is comparable to k-means clustering that was supplied with the true number of participants (0.88). We also examined PCA dimensionality, modality availability, and variation strength, and demonstrated the model on a Toyota Human Support Robot. These results show that multimodal person concept learning supports robust person identification under changing conditions, and that identification can succeed even when the number of concepts is not correctly recovered. The project page and demonstration video are available at https://okitamisan01.github.io/person_concept/.

title: Resource Management and Trajectory Optimization for UAV-IRS Assisted Maritime Edge Computing Networks
summary: With the exponential growth of maritime wireless devices and the rapid development of maritime applications, traditional maritime communication networks encounter communication and computation limitations in supporting computation-intensive and latency-critical tasks. Edge computing and Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) have emerged as promising techniques to improve communication and computation services for maritime devices with limited computation capabilities and battery capacity. This paper studies an IRS Mounted on Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UIRS) assisted maritime edge computing network, in which the UIRS is deployed to assist the transmission from Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USVs) to the edge server via Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) protocol. We propose a resource management and trajectory optimization scheme by jointly optimizing subslot duration, offloading ratios, transmit power, edge computation capability allocation, UIRS phase shifts and UIRS trajectory, aiming at minimizing the overall energy consumption. Since the non-convex nature of the optimization problem, we propose a two-layered method by decomposing the original problem into two subproblems. The top-layered subproblem is solved by the Semi-Definite Relaxation (SDR) method and the underlying-layered subproblem is solved by the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm. Numerical results demonstrate that our proposed scheme can effectively and efficiently reduce overall energy consumption.

title: Can Agents Keep Up with Time? An Empirical Analysis of Temporal Adaptation After a Conversational Hiatus
summary: Long-horizon agents increasingly serve as persistent personal assistants across modern web platforms, managing schedules, applications, and multi-step plans over weeks or months. Users often return to an ongoing conversation after a long conversational hiatus, while earlier bookings and preparation notes stay on record. During this hiatus, scheduled dates may pass even though the retained records remain unchanged and event outcomes go unrecorded. Existing evaluations of long-horizon agents focus on fact retention and explicit state updates. Whether agents perceive the passage of time and adapt their advice accordingly therefore remains unknown. We frame this ability as temporal state perception and use, which means perceiving the current time and applying it when interpreting dated records. To study it, we design session-rekindling tasks that keep the earlier conversation fixed and vary only the follow-up date and the way temporal information reaches the agent. Experiments across five model routes and five temporal-information conditions show that agents can obtain the current time but often fail to use it. They reliably query the clock and even note in their reasoning that the scheduled date has passed, yet many still tell users to prepare for the expired event. Supplying explicit temporal context reduces this error, and providing the computed date relation removes it entirely. Keeping up with time therefore depends on turning perceived time into updated plans. Based on these findings, we design a session-rekindling benchmark that provides temporal-awareness guidance for designing long-horizon agents. The code can be found at https://github.com/Adoreu2/session-rekindling-benchmark.

title: CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: $S_α$ prioritizes task success while accounting for resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS) measures the resources spent per successful task. Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM Actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.7 percentage points. It also achieves the best average scores on both metrics.

title: AI Reviews Are Biased Towards the Appendix
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by reviewers to highlight weaknesses during the reviewing process, and their outputs often shape the reviews that humans submit. Prior work studies how LLM reviews align with human ones, yet we know little about which parts of a paper these models actually criticize. In this work, we investigate 2,000 papers from ACL, EMNLP, COLM, and ICLR, and show that the latest GPT and Claude models draw about 50% or more of their review weaknesses from the appendix. This behavior holds across the API, coding-agent, and web access methods for using LLMs to review a paper. In contrast, we find that humans draw only 8.4% of their weaknesses from the appendix, and these weaknesses primarily revolve around a paper's presentation and content related to its core idea. Meanwhile, LLMs draw weaknesses from deep in the appendix that concern fine-grained technical details not central to the paper's contributions. We anticipate that our analysis will contribute to the scholarly discourse on AI reviews. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/cincynlp/review_appendix.

title: G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands
summary: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), an increasing number of users are turning to LLM-powered agents for conversational shopping in e-commerce. However, the user needs continue to change as new product categories, procurement scenarios, and feature requests emerge. At the same time, the product's execution harness-including its tools, skills, and operating procedures-continues to evolve to support increasingly sophisticated interactions. These changes create two practical challenges: 1) Demand drift alters the distribution, intent, and complexity of user requests, causing a model trained once to fall behind; 2) Harness evolution requires the model to use newly introduced capabilities correctly without losing behavior that users already rely on. Periodic manual retraining is too delayed and labor-intensive for this setting. To address these challenges, we present G-CAST, a governed continual self-training system that converts daily production evidence under evolving demand and capability contracts into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data and governed reward evolution. Governed checkpoint transition under cumulative evaluation controls each model update, enabling the agent to learn newly introduced behaviors without sacrificing previously accepted capabilities. Experiments on a real production e-commerce agent show that G-CAST achieves stronger adaptation to newly introduced demand while better preserving previously accepted behavior compared with a strong autonomous post-training baseline. Ablations further show that both reward-routed, entropy-prioritized data orchestration and governed reward evolution are important to these gains. G-CAST is now deployed in Yuancai(http://cai.1688.com/), a B2B procurement agent on Alibaba's 1688 platform.

title: Quantum Shock and Train-Time Constrained Quantization: A Geometric Study of Finite-Resolution Variational Quantum Circuits
summary: Finite-resolution interfaces map Variational-Circuit angle to discrete codebook. Since Pauli rotations are periodic, so Euclidean rounding may produce wrong codeword near a chart boundary; error due to coordinates alone cannot measure how much the final state was changed. Herein we define a metric, Quantum Shock, for Pure State it is defined as the average of the square of the Fubini-Study distance (over all inputs) between the pre-deployment and deployed states. This value is limited by constant multipliers of the mean of infidelity and provides upper limits on displacement when observing bounded quantities and margin based predictive stability. Extensions to the analytical Bures-angle for mixed-states were derived, along with a finite shot stability bound. The proposed Train-Time Constrained Quantization allows a delay in applying a penalty for selecting a codeword aligned with periodicity until after task only optimizations. Three small binary tasks were evaluated on a four qubit, two layer classifier using ten matched seeds, K = 4, 8, 16 and exact expectation values from simulation under noiseless conditions and state vector simulations. On our primary evaluation, T-CQ exhibited smaller average local quantum shock compared to circular post-training quantization for each task and code-book size tested. The re-execution on the x86-64 platform using K=8 preserved the direction of the mean-shock comparison but had varying magnitudes.

title: LLMs are Vulnerable to Malicious Requests with Indistinguishable Intent
summary: Jailbreak attacks can circumvent the safety mechanisms of Large Language Models (LLMs) and lead to the generation of harmful or policy-violating content. We first examine eight jailbreak methods against an LLM-based filter and observe that requests resembling normal user queries tend to have higher filter pass rates than those containing obvious anomalous patterns. This observation motivates the hypothesis that resemblance to normal requests may contribute to jailbreak success. We introduce \textbf{Detail Guidance Attack (DGA)}, a framework that uses an auxiliary LLM to construct detailed requests and interacts with the victim model in a single turn. Across 11 victim models and three datasets, the complete DGA pipeline achieves high attack success rates under our automated judging criterion, including rates above 95\% in several evaluated settings. We also evaluate a DGA-aware filter and conduct a user study on everyday requests with ambiguous or dual-use intent. The survey documents differing expectations about whether models should respond; the usability costs of the filter remain to be measured.

title: Causally Constrained and Uncertainty-Aware Cardiopulmonary Risk Prediction
summary: Routine chest computed tomography (CT) captures pulmonary, cardiac, and vascular phenotypes that jointly stratify lung cancer and cardiovascular disease, the two leading causes of death in lung-screening populations. Yet clinical risk calculators evaluate each disease in isolation and omit CT findings, whereas unconstrained machine learning overfits small hospital cohorts, learns treatment- and illness-confounded risk directions, and conceals uncertainty when patient records are incomplete. Here we present the Causal Envelope Agent (CE-Agent), a two-stage framework that compiles peer-reviewed epidemiological evidence into explicit constraints on risk-factor weights before any outcome is seen, while estimating local baseline risk and newly added CT phenotypes from cohort data. At deployment, closed-form uncertainty propagation accounts for missing clinical or CT inputs within milliseconds per patient, running over two orders of magnitude faster than Monte Carlo sampling and returning calibrated risk intervals that direct chart review and selective imaging to borderline patients. Across 53,452 lung-screening participants from 33 US hospitals and 6,814 multi-ethnic adults, CE-Agent outperforms cardiovascular calculators in lung screening, exceeds the Pooled Cohort Equations on hard atherosclerotic events while correcting their 1.7-fold risk overestimation, and generalizes from a single hospital or CT scanner to external sites while lowering required sample sizes up to fivefold. Applied unchanged to lung cancer, CE-Agent matches established screening models with accurate calibration even when restricted to risk-factor directions alone, and pairing both predictions improves joint cardiopulmonary triage from a single screening visit.

title: Aligning AI Teams
summary: Previous work has shown that alignment training on individual LLM agents can fail to transfer to multi-agent settings. We investigate the underlying mechanisms for this failure, and explore interventions to preserve alignment transfer to multi-agent LLM teams. We focus on two software-engineering tasks (sepsis triage, a news recommender) and ten consulting-proposal generation tasks. We present four findings: (1) The single-vs-team safety gap does not show a clear trend with more capable models. We find that Anthropic's Mythos Preview shows the largest gap on one of our tasks but the smallest on another; (2) Many natural interventions, such as having agents critique each other's work or coordinate in a group chat, do not reliably bring agent teams back to single-agent alignment behavior; (3) diffusion of responsibility substantially accounts for the safety gap: agents in teams are less likely to proactively check for system-level safety failures and more likely to ignore, rationalize, or deflect responsibility for issues when they arise; (4) having a designated safety lead agent ensure system-level safety, and having a coordinator agent publish a safety specifications document are effective at restoring single-agent alignment. We also release magelab, a multi-agent LLM orchestration and experimentation framework.
